title: Trump’s October Surprise
excerpt: I t rained most of Sunday in Washington, as the remnants of Hurricane Isaias washed over the East Coast
body: I t rained most of Sunday in Washington, as the remnants of Hurricane Isaias washed over the East Coast
Unable to golf, and stuck inside the White House, President Trump spent part of his morning on social media touting the size of his rallies and defending Christopher Columbus
He also declared that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt strikes against each other’s energy infrastructures

Except that he hadn’t first confirmed that with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky—and Russia spent the hours that followed bombarding Ukraine with missiles and drones, hitting a Kharkiv power plant
Trump’s inability to bring the Iran war to a close has left him incensed but also oddly paralyzed, two people close to him told us

One of them, an adviser, said that Trump “is used to snapping his fingers and having the whole world—Republicans, world leaders, the media—come to attention, and he is losing his mind that Iran won’t listen.” Iran has resumed menacing oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, and the average price of diesel in the United States has crossed the $6-a-gallon mark, raising the cost of goods that travel the nation’s highways on trucks
Republicans are panicked that those high energy prices could help Democrats take control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections, which are now only three weeks away
Trump has been searching for a scapegoat, and appears to have settled on Ukraine

Although blaming a European country that’s fighting for its existence for the rise in global oil prices might seem implausible, Trump seems to prefer that to accepting responsibility for his decision to attack Iran
His broadsides against Ukraine, moreover, are consistent with his decade-long deference to Vladimir Putin
With rare exceptions, Trump has aligned with Moscow over Kyiv throughout the four-and-a-half-year war
He wants Ukraine to end the fighting—and has pressured the country to agree to terms that Zelensky finds unacceptable
A U.S. president siding with the Kremlin is quite an October surprise
But in just the past few days, Trump appears to have fully turned against Ukraine

He announced on Friday that he had reached an agreement with Putin to import Russian diesel fuel, undercutting the new sanctions bill against Moscow’s energy industry that Trump signed into law last month

Even if the roughly 2.25 million barrels headed to the U.S. only marginally ease fuel costs, the deal allows Trump to tout efforts to help Americans while also providing Russia with additional revenue. (Another few million barrels are set to ship next month.) Despite the opposition of European allies and some Republicans on Capitol Hill, Trump has followed up by placing even more pressure on Ukraine
His aides have threatened to withhold arms sales unless Kyiv stops targeting Russian diesel plants
Some in Trump’s orbit have suggested that the U.S. go further, and stop sharing intelligence with Kyiv
That was the context in which Trump announced his fictional energy cease-fire

A senior Ukrainian military officer told us that Trump’s statements are “simply beyond comprehension.” “Things are already incredibly difficult for us here,” the officer said, speaking, like others who talked with us, on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters. “But apparently, there’s always another level below rock bottom
Things can always get worse.” U kraine has expanded its strikes deep into Russian territory in recent months, targeting the larger nation’s oil refineries
Those attacks sparked an energy crisis in Russia and were cheered across Europe—but not in the White House
Russia imposed a ban on diesel exports in response, which added more pressure to global diesel markets already under strain from the war in Iran

Zelensky told Trump and his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner that he was willing to stop attacking Russian oil refineries if the Russians halted attacks on Ukrainian power plants, a White House official told us
But Trump doesn’t see the strikes as equivalent—and demanded that Ukraine first stop attacking Russian refineries, the official said
Zelensky refused. “Zelensky is overplaying his hand and pissing the president off,” the White House official said. “The president is asking for one thing: stop hitting the refineries
Give him that.” [ Read: Trump’s latest appeal to Russia could outrage even his allies ] Trump’s next move against Ukraine came, as it so often does, after a phone call with Putin

Zelensky’s aides have expressed frustration that Putin has swayed Trump at crucial junctures in the conflict (once, even, while Zelensky was flying to Washington to meet with Trump in an effort to secure access to new U.S. weapons)
This time, Trump spoke with Putin on Friday to wish him a belated birthday, even though some in the White House counseled against the call, the adviser told us, believing it would yield little

During the 90-minute conversation, Trump told Putin that he would lift the sanctions on Russian diesel exports. (Some in Kyiv believe that the deal was agreed to earlier, because a ship carrying Russian oil and gas is already approaching the U.S.) That undermined sanctions applied in 2022 and undercut the tougher Russian-sanctions bill that Trump signed last month; the law was named in honor of one of its champions, the late Senator Lindsey Graham
A bipartisan group of lawmakers was infuriated by the move, and some Republicans denounced Trump for siding with Putin

Four GOP senators—Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Susan Collins of ⁠Maine, Thom Tillis of North Carolina, and John Curtis of Utah—joined some of their Democratic colleagues to release a statement yesterday saying that lifting the sanctions “runs directly counter to that law” and that the U.S. should not provide “Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians.” Zelensky, who was blindsided by the diesel deal, deemed it “not fair and not honest.” He had spent more than a year trying to repair his relationship with Trump, which hit its nadir in February 2025 during a shouting match in the Oval Office
Since then, Zelensky has taken to flattering the U.S. president, and he has tried to capitalize on Trump’s occasional annoyance that Putin will not end the war
Trump and Putin’s Alaska summit last year yielded little more than a photo of the two that hangs in the Palm Room at the White House
Even if Trump wouldn’t fully support Ukraine, officials in Kyiv had hoped he would not actively hurt their cause
Recent talks between Kushner, Witkoff, and Putin have included the promise of massive business deals that Russia could strike with U.S. interests once the war concludes, according to reports

Ukrainian officials have long believed that Trump’s foreign policy focuses on opening up business deals—and the potential enrichment of the president’s family and friends—over the defense of democracy, human rights, or territorial sovereignty
Some officials in Kyiv believe that Russia’s economy, which has been remade to fuel Putin’s war machine, will not implode, despite the pressure of increased drone strikes and sanctions
A Ukrainian official close to the negotiating process told us that means “we need to change our strategy, stop fooling ourselves,” and find a way out of the war with Europe’s help
That, the official said, would likely require a new emphasis on negotiations

title: Trump’s Message to Ukraine Is Now Crystal Clear
excerpt: In the past 72 hours, Donald Trump has dropped all pretense, torched a couple decades of American policy, and undermined 18 months of his own diplomacy
body: In the past 72 hours, Donald Trump has dropped all pretense, torched a couple decades of American policy, and undermined 18 months of his own diplomacy
He lifted sanctions on the import of Russian diesel fuel, in violation of the letter and spirit of laws that he himself signed

He has threatened to stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine, unless Ukraine agrees not to target Russian refineries, thus demanding that Kyiv give up its most effective weapon while asking nothing from Russia in exchange
He has not criticized Russian attacks on Ukrainian power plants or factories, even those owned by American companies
He has offered no condolences for the recent deaths of Ukrainian children in Russian bombing raids

He declared that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an “energy cease-fire,” an announcement that surprised the Ukrainians and that in any case the Russians immediately broke, hitting a power plant in Kharkiv only hours later
He accused Ukraine of blocking negotiations, when in reality the Ukrainians have repeatedly proposed cease-fires and Russia has never agreed to a cease-fire or any meaningful negotiation at all
He has described Ukraine’s democratically elected president as an obstacle to negotiations and told him to leave office
But on Friday, before making these new decisions, he held yet another long, friendly telephone conversation with the Russian dictator, who really could end the war today
All Vladimir Putin has to do is tell his soldiers to stop fighting, and then the war is over

The Ukrainians cannot stop fighting because, if they do, their country will be conquered and they will suffer the fate of their occupied territories: leaders murdered, children kidnapped, repression and concentration camps for everyone else
If Trump knows this, then he does not care. [ David Frum: Trump is an easy mark for Putin ] The president has implied that the point of his new policy is to lower fuel prices for Americans
Perhaps he wants to convince voters that the cause of high prices is Ukraine and not his own war of choice in Iran
But this is not a sufficient explanation or justification for these dramatic actions
The amount of fuel that Russia could export is too small, the impact on pricing too slight, the narrative too late to shape electoral outcomes

This looks, instead, like something very different: an abrupt, Hail Mary attempt to force Ukraine to surrender and to save the Russian economy, perhaps in order to finally complete the multiple business deals that the Russians are known to have discussed with American negotiators and others in Trump’s orbit
These include deals involving the Nord Stream gas pipelines, mineral mining in the Arctic, the Russian assets frozen in European banks, and more

Since the beginning of Trump’s second term, American allies in Europe and elsewhere have tried to explain to the president the significance of the war and the threat that Russia poses to peace and prosperity in Europe, in the Middle East, in Africa
Now it looks as if they have failed, and Trump has followed his oldest instincts to side with Putin
What lessons will they draw? The first and most obvious is: Don’t rely on the United States
America is now a capricious, unpredictable power, one whose long-standing foreign policies can be impulsively reversed, from one day to the next
The U.S. has been sanctioning Russia for many years, and now suddenly, at the whim of the president, it is not
Also: Dictators receive better treatment in Trump’s Washington than elected leaders
Canada is a far more reliable energy partner for the U.S. than Russia, and yet Trump has not sought to improve relations with the Canadian government
European security will be directly at risk in the case of a Ukrainian collapse or surrender, and yet Trump listens to Moscow, not Berlin or London
Another lesson: This administration is for sale

A few days ago, The New York Times reported that, as part of peace negotiations between the U.S. and Russia, the property of Lukoil, a Russian company, may soon be acquired by a business consortium that includes Middle Eastern partners of Trump’s two lead negotiators in Ukraine, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, as well as Trump’s daughter Ivanka and Witkoff’s son. (An administration official confirmed to the Times that Kushner and Witkoff were involved in the Lukoil discussions, though there is no evidence that they will personally benefit.) The proposed deals on pipelines, minerals, and frozen assets are also still on the table

Even if none of them is ever completed, the mere fact that Trump’s negotiators discuss them gives the Russian regime reason to believe that it can continue the war with impunity. [ Read: Trump’s latest appeal to Russia could outrage even his allies ] However, democracies can cooperate without the American president
Ukraine will continue fighting, and will probably continue striking Russian refineries, thanks to its friends in Europe and beyond
French intelligence, German weaponry, and broad packages of aid from Scandinavia, Poland, and elsewhere will help
For the past couple years, Europeans, Canadians, and the Pacific democracies have been building deeper commercial and security links with one another, as well as with India and Latin America
They’ve just been given another reason to make those links stronger
The Trump-Russia relationship remains intense, important, and very weird
In the end, Trump always adopts Russia’s perspective, whoever the leader
Since his first trip to Moscow in 1987, when it was still the Soviet Union, he has loudly repeated Russian propaganda and reflected Russian views
Upon returning from that trip, he took out full-page advertisements in three newspapers, attacking American alliances in Europe and Asia
For nearly 40 years, he has been saying much the same thing

He has changed his mind about abortion and crypto, he has supported different political parties at different times, but his dislike of America’s democratic allies and his preference for Russia have remained remarkably consistent
He continues to hold these views in defiance of the American military and American intelligence, as well as majorities in the country and in Congress
Immediately after his statement on diesel and his comments about Volodymyr Zelensky, a bipartisan cohort of U.S. representatives and senators attacked the deal and vowed to reverse it

title: Make Big Brother Bad for Big Business
excerpt: Garrett Langley, the founder and CEO of Flock Safety, is an unlikely spokesperson for the dangers of the surveillance industry: His company says it has deployed
body: Garrett Langley, the founder and CEO of Flock Safety, is an unlikely spokesperson for the dangers of the surveillance industry: His company says it has deployed more than 120,000 roadside cameras across 49 states
But in August, while defending his products and policies, he perhaps inadvertently showed why Americans should be alarmed by this technology

Flock caught “a ton” of “bad cops” when it rolled out a tool to identify abuse of its data, Langley acknowledged on the All-In podcast. (While Flock will soon require the tool for all of its law-enforcement clients, just a fraction of clients were using it as of mid-August

Many bad cops likely went uncaught.) He argued that Flock will force safeguards on clients, though that may lose the company business, because he wants to “sleep at night.” His competitors, meanwhile, “run more reckless”—offering video and facial recognition with their license-plate readers, for example
If you take him at his word—and I’d argue that he overstates the strength of Flock’s safeguards––it’s clear that the way the industry works is worrying even one of its biggest boosters
My own sleep has been troubled by the private surveillance industry for more than a decade
In 2014, three years before Flock was founded, I warned in The Atlantic that mass surveillance of all car trips was nearly upon us

I noted that private companies were deploying automatic license-plate readers, or ALPRs, at scale on America’s public roads, threatening a privacy we’ve always enjoyed, and that Congress should regulate the fast-growing surveillance industry
Today, if you drive in much of the continental United States, Flock may profit by selling others the means to reconstruct your movements

Opposition to this form of surveillance is now a plurality position, according to an August YouGov survey , which found that more Americans oppose the technology’s use in their neighborhood than support it
Politicians in both major parties are criticizing ALPRs, whose name has become something of a misnomer: The cameras can capture detailed images of passing vehicles, not just of the license plate

And anti-Flock activists who track clients of the company list scores of past and potential clients that have canceled their contracts or deactivated cameras in recent months. “I’ve never really seen such a grassroots uprising against surveillance technology,” Jay Stanley, an ACLU senior policy analyst, told The Guardian . “On the left, there’s a historical memory of law enforcement spying on and interfering with advocates for social change … On the right, there’s a long tradition of ‘don’t tread on me’—keep the government out of my life, keep it from looking over my shoulder.” Still, most of Flock’s network and its competitors’ cameras remain in place

And fans of the technology want to keep it that way; they argue that there is no reasonable expectation of privacy on roads, and that a network of cameras that logs every passing vehicle is a vital tool for catching criminals
Most surveillance boosters don’t deny that serious abuses have happened or wholly dismiss privacy concerns
Instead, they urge the use of safeguards and the passage of regulations to address them
But this technology is already ubiquitous
States and localities should not permit its dangers to persist in the hope that one day, our often passive legislators will act
Instead, Americans should work to ban mass surveillance of public roads in every jurisdiction where they can secure support from elected officials until strong protections are in place
The pro-surveillance coalition has significant political influence, and some of its members employ accomplished lobbyists
The only way that it will hasten privacy safeguards is if doing so is the only way to sustain the surveillance business
Before sketching out what specific legislative protections could look like, it’s helpful to notice that popular debates about ALPRs overstate their likely benefits and understate their dangers
The primary benefit––they help catch some criminals––will grow less effective over time as knowledge of the technology and how to evade it spreads
For example, license plates are already being cloned
And as the benefits decline, the cost that law-abiding citizens pay in lost privacy will persist
After all, the business model–– pay us and we’ll help you catch criminals ––creates a powerful incentive for surveillance companies to address falling effectiveness with new privacy intrusions
Flock may eschew facial recognition today, but no federal law prevents it from changing its mind tomorrow, or requires that it alert the public before introducing a new tool

While evidence remains limited that ALPRs reduce crime in general or violent crime in particular, there is solid evidence that they reduce car theft: A working paper , published in August by the criminologists Scott M

Adams, found that ALPR networks are associated with an 11 percent decline in such thefts and an increase in arrest clearance (though they cautioned that clearances were already rising in the weeks before camera deployment)
But if vehicle owners installed their own trackers, benefits could be had for all who opt in without imposing costs on everyone’s privacy
Some dangers of roadside cameras are well understood
The Institute for Justice maintains a database of known and alleged police abuses of the technology , including stalking and wrongful stops

And although Flock’s rollout of Audit Assistance, the tool that helps catch abuse by cops, redounds to the company’s credit, it is no cure-all: It “detects abnormal activity and flags it for Administrator review,” a Flock spokesperson clarified to me by email, which “refers to review by an authorized administrator at the customer agency—not a Flock administrator.” This leaves open the possibility that abuse will remain undisciplined by some police departments
A less widely understood danger is what might be called the foreign-adversary problem
China, Russia, and others have real incentives for gaining access to data collected by license-plate readers
Doing so could assist hostile actors in recruiting assets, blackmail, intimidation, and more
Breaching Flock would be the biggest prize––and the public is in no position to evaluate how competently the company or its competitors secure their data
If Edward Snowden could make off with the NSA’s most sensitive secrets, a systems administrator at Flock or a competitor could theoretically attempt a large-scale theft
The company (let alone the public) may not even know about it
That worst-case scenario aside, a hostile foreign actor could do damage to U.S. interests merely via the access that normal Flock clients enjoy
Thousands of law-enforcement agencies use Flock

title: The Tragedy of AI Coding
excerpt: My family and I enjoy the occasional meal of delicious slow-cooked meat, but every time we visit a barbecue joint, we can’t remember whether we like the beans a
body: My family and I enjoy the occasional meal of delicious slow-cooked meat, but every time we visit a barbecue joint, we can’t remember whether we like the beans and slaw on offer
Some slaw is vinegar based; others creamy
We should keep track of this somehow , we always say but then never bother
Thanks to generative artificial intelligence, it became less ridiculous
By last summer, I had been making small programs with AI for some time
AI’s adeptness at programming was helping me, a busy person with a professional programming background but limited reason to program, work creatively with computing for the first time in ages
I wanted to see how far I could push AI as a solo programmer

The barbecue-sides-preference problem, I reasoned, would serve as a perfect test case: building a fully featured iPhone app—Beanslaw, I called it—with esoteric utility that nobody would have bothered commercializing
Two days of occasional programming were sufficient to make a professional-grade version of Beanslaw—an act that would have taken weeks of full-time dedication not long ago
The app displayed smoked-meat joints on a searchable map
It implemented sophisticated intelligence to filter out Korean barbecue, Brazilian churrasco , and other (no less delectable!) cuisines that entail barbecue of a different, bean-and-slawless variety
A user can assign assessments of beans (such as vegetarian and soupy) and slaw (including chunky and mustard), and filter the map by desired side-dish traits
Photos courtesy of the author Excited, I showed a friend. “Where are everyone else’s slaw and bean ratings?” he asked, tapping at his phone
He didn’t get the point of an app that amounted to a personal journal
Almost two decades of smartphone apps had trained him to understand software as a mechanism for collective intelligence
A program that only a few people would use is now alien

App has come to refer to a type of global, leveraged software business, not a computer program. [ Josh Tyrangiel: The secret to understanding AI ] Because AI is so good at writing software, in only an hour or so, I was able to add community ratings
Now Beanslaw does what my friend would expect it to—connect potentially billions of users
But doing so also turned an idiosyncratic app meant to satisfy me alone into a candidate (a hopeless one, at that) for the software attention economy

But during the year since, I have written, with AI’s aid, a dozen or more programs to solve anomalous problems, seeking to understand what AI programming—a practice some people call vibe coding —means for computing culture
AI-assisted coding could revive the old dream of ordinary people making software for themselves

But so far, in practice it amounts to a new trip down an old path that software development has been traversing for decades: one where a privileged few decide what computers are for, and the rest of us fall in line

In the early 1960s, inspired by Vannevar Bush’s 1945 Atlantic essay “ As We May Think ,” a recent Swarthmore College philosophy graduate named Ted Nelson began conceptualizing a computer-publishing system for all global knowledge, accessible to anyone—work for which he coined the term hypertext
A decade later, in 1974, Nelson expanded his vision of computing’s populist power in a pamphlet manifesto called Computer Lib/Dream Machines
At the time, computers were big, expensive machines used by corporations and government offices

Before the personal computer arrived in earnest, Nelson denounced the “appalling gap between public and computer insider.” He characterized the corporate and governmental actors with access to and expertise in computing as a “priesthood.” Nelson advocated for dismantling this priesthood and putting computing in the hands of ordinary people

Nelson, along with other figures of the personal-computer revolution, saw his work as literally revolutionary: The Lib of Computer Lib referred to liberation, like “women’s lib,” and he and his allies understood their work as a part of the counterculture movement
Seymour Papert, who co-designed the programming language Logo , envisioned programming as a way for kids to control these machines rather than submit to them

Inspired by Papert, Alan Kay imagined the tablet-style Dynabook, a “ personal computer for children of all ages .” And Steve Wozniak, who designed the first Apple (and co-founded Apple Computer with Steve Jobs), valued cheap, publicly shared software skills as a way to overthrow the corporate monopoly on computing
For a time, that liberationist vision became reality
Early personal computers such as the Apple II and Commodore 64 booted up to a command prompt where users could immediately begin programming in BASIC, an intuitive language
Early advertisements pitched them explicitly as devices people could program themselves
Computer magazines of the era published code that readers typed into their machines by hand
I learned Papert’s Logo as a first grader in the early 1980s, because my private school had invested in personal computers, labs to house them, and teachers to guide us
That head start gave me confidence with computer programming, which was presented as a normal activity akin to making art or reading
I picked up BASIC, assembly, Pascal, C, and other languages naturally
The machines couldn’t do much yet, and I could learn new things as they evolved—which was still slow enough that an ordinary person, even a child, could keep up
Personal though they might have become, computers remained expensive and largely inaccessible
And the relatively well-off people who bought them were more likely to buy commercial software than to write their own
Within a few years, the graphical user interface popularized by Macintosh and Windows made the machines easier to use yet also more complicated

title: The People Who Outsource Emotional Labor to AI
excerpt: One day not long ago, Franky, a 40-something woman who lives in the mid-Atlantic region, got an infuriating text message from her aunt
body: One day not long ago, Franky, a 40-something woman who lives in the mid-Atlantic region, got an infuriating text message from her aunt
It was just the latest truth-stretching missive she had sent, and Franky’s impulse was to write back: “You’re a liar

All you do is lie.” Instead, she asked an AI program to write a response that was less “condescending and unnecessarily emotional.” AI-ese, Franky told me, helps make her responses more logical and neutral
Another message that she sent her aunt after running it through a chatbot read, “I respect you and I expect the same in return
I want to have a mature conversation.” The aunt appreciated it, Franky said—she called her and sounded calm
Franky is among a number of people—we’ll never truly know how many, will we?—who secretly use AI programs such as ChatGPT and Claude when they interact with difficult family members

Mostly, my interviewees use AI to communicate with individuals they don’t want an emotionally close relationship with—an ex they co-parent with, for example, or an in-law—but whom they nevertheless can’t escape. (Because they are describing tense personal relations, most of my interviewees requested not to be identified by their full name.) People use AI to both interpret messages they receive and help them write their own to send

If they have to, say, call out rude behavior or express disagreement about whether the kids need a certain type of therapy, they type what they really want to say into one of these programs, ask the AI to nice it up a little, and paste the resulting verbiage into their text messages
Outsourcing correspondence to AI has enabled them to maintain harmony without spending too much time thinking about how to draft a perfect response

As Franky put it, using AI lets her have a relationship without allowing it to “live rent-free in my brain.” Franky said that in her family, it’s important for people “all to have, I don’t know, peace.” She and others have found that they can improve their relationships and at least increase the probability of peace by removing emotion from conversations

And that’s where AI truly excels. [ Read: There’s a name for the people who drain you ] Another woman I spoke with told me about how Claude had helped her revise a text to a family member who often misinterprets her words
This person, she said, sent her a message implying that he wanted her out of his life
Her impulse was to reply, “Congratulations

You got your wish,” but Claude softened that statement because it could “read as sarcasm/implication.” Then it asked, “Want it warmer, blunter, or shorter still?” Claude, she added, “leaves out the emotional part” and makes it more likely that the recipient will hear her and work toward a resolution

People reach for Cyrano de Anthropic because during difficult text-based conversations, “it’s hard to know what to say,” Nedra Glover Tawwab, a therapist and the author, most recently, of The Balancing Act , told me
When we’re interacting in person, mechanisms in the brain help us interpret people’s body language and facial expressions, Matthew Fishleder, a therapist in Maryland, told me

But text and email strip messages of that context. “We’re left trying to decipher, What does this text from my mom mean? ” he said. “ And how in the world do I respond to something like this? ” In tense situations, people generally know what they’d like to express, Tawwab said, but then they might think, “ I can’t say that .” AI can phrase the message in a slightly gentler way—and it can offer the sender “less of a responsibility” for how the recipient reacts
If your mom gets mad about your AI-assisted message, you can always mentally blame Dario Amodei

The most common use case I encountered for deploying AI in this way was to correspond calmly with an ex-spouse, whom one may now resent with the fire of a thousand billable lawyer hours but whom one must treat cordially, lest one gets threatened with changes to the custody agreement. (As one Florida woman who uses AI for this purpose told me, sending an “F you” text to your ex might feel amazing, but you have to think about the “legal ramifications.”) A father in Arizona told ChatGPT to use a “five-star-hotel-clerk tone” with his ex, and it did—to the point that, reading over his shoulder, his child was shocked by how nice their parents were being to each other
A woman who asked to go by the initial S. told me that she uses AI to negotiate co-parenting decisions with her ex-partner

When AI helps her write “in a very neutral tone so that it’s not inflaming,” she said, “we help our kids to the best degree possible.” She told me that the tool has improved her relationship with her ex-partner, and that she even sometimes recommends the same strategy to her clients in her work as a therapist
If their exes figure out that they’re using AI, many of the people I spoke with don’t really care
S. thinks her ex may be using it too, because sometimes she’ll notice that “that’s a tone I don’t hear very often from him,” she said
The Florida woman said that her ex has accused her of using AI “many times” but that she’s not especially concerned about impressing him. “It’s like, Oh, I know
I’m terrible in every way, including that I use AI ,” she said. “Add it to the list
We get it.’” The people I spoke with had a range of other reasons for using AI

Several of my interviewees are not native English speakers, and they feel that they are frequently misunderstood when they use their own words. “Even when I do try my absolute best, it just doesn’t work,” the Arizona father told me
One of the people he has used AI to communicate with is an abusive parent; given his childhood environment, he said, he doesn’t have much experience being spoken to amiably and calmly

Others don’t have much experience with writing, period: A woman named Ashleigh told me that she uses ChatGPT to communicate with her baby’s father’s family because she’s “not a writer at all.” She said that she types in what she wants to say, then prompts the system to “take some of the emotion out and put more of the facts in it.” “It’s great for hard conversations,” she added, “that you know you’re gonna blow up on.” Finally, many of my interviewees like how much time AI saves them
They don’t want to spend their one wild and precious life drafting heartfelt texts to their weird cousin; they want to outsource all of that to Claude

As Franky put it to me, in one of the most relatable quotes I have ever gathered, “I just don’t have time in general to do anything.” [ Read: Forgive the bad texters ] Using a robot to talk with humans has downsides, of course, even if only philosophical ones
Relying on AI for communication can mean that we are “outsourcing our inner power to a machine,” Tawwab said
The people I spoke with are well aware of that

Even though she uses it herself, S. said that her therapy clients can become overly dependent on AI, to the point where they “aren’t thinking for themselves as much.” But as far as mortal sins go, this practice seems to fall somewhere around ordering from Amazon Prime or eating at McDonald’s—you may have misgivings, but the convenience truly can’t be beat

Fishleder, the Maryland therapist, said that although AI can be helpful in a pinch, it won’t resolve the larger relationship dynamics at issue—and it’s further evidence of what he characterized as the “movement away from relying on one another as humans.” Still, when I asked him whether he also sometimes uses AI to write tricky messages, he said, “100 percent.” Sometimes you just need to send a firm but polite text about Thanksgiving plans
It’s not cheating; it’s muddling through.

title: Immigration Is a Poorly Oiled Machine
excerpt: W hat would the U.S. immigration system look like if it were a machine, made of wheels and gears, controlled by belts and joints? In Kelly Lytle Hernández’s new
body: W hat would the U.S. immigration system look like if it were a machine, made of wheels and gears, controlled by belts and joints? In Kelly Lytle Hernández’s new book, Racist by Design: Two Centuries of U.S
Immigration Control , illustrations by the artist Mariah Tso help readers visualize such a contraption
Its parts are etched with important names and dates, Supreme Court cases, racist proclamations, and key concepts such as eugenics, no due process, and warrantless arrests
These sketches leave the impression that immigration control functions smoothly to exclude certain people—requiring only the occasional application of oil or glue
I would depict this machine differently, as would many historians
Its parts would be misaligned and mismatched; it would leak and spew smoke, expand and contract at random, and periodically grind to a halt

Yet Tso’s illustrations perfectly reflect the argument made by Lytle Hernández, a history professor at UCLA whose previous books have focused on the Border Patrol , mass incarceration , and Mexican anarchists

In Racist by Design , she contends that the United States since its founding has had a “whites-only immigration system.” That system has evolved, she says, but it remains “racist by design: It always has been and it still is.” We shouldn’t take “whites-only” literally, Lytle Hernández cautions

Instead, she writes, the term is an “interpretive device” to help us understand “racialized power.” She borrows language from the book Let This Radicalize You , in which two organizers, Kelly Hayes and Mariame Kaba, argue for studying a machine to figure out “what blows could actually disable it.” Lytle Hernández wants Racist by Design to land as a blow propelled by the force of history, inspiring collective action that will “keep pushing” the machine “and make it tip.” [ Read: What Stephen Miller gets wrong about human nature ] It isn’t controversial to say that racism has often motivated American immigration policy
Stephen Miller , Trump’s senior aide and homeland-security adviser, is hardly the first nativist to set federal priorities
Yet Lytle Hernández’s contention that more than two centuries of immigration control boil down to a story of white supremacy is an overstatement, even if it’s an important provocation

Lytle Hernández briefly acknowledges that “whiteness” isn’t always a simple category—that eugenicists have invented hierarchies among white people, and that racially neutral language, such as the word pauper , has been used to deport Irish people
But she doesn’t discuss how the meaning of whiteness changed over time; some white people were considered less white than others

She mentions other factors in debates over who can enter the country—sexuality, religion, public health, international diplomacy, ideology—but brushes them aside quickly so that they don’t muddy her point

These omissions and elisions make her argument vulnerable to challenges not only from historians who have studied other modes of discrimination, but also from political opponents eager to sabotage her cause
P lenty of evidence supports Lytle Hernández’s larger case
The Naturalization Act of 1790 said that only “a free white person” could naturalize, after living in the United States for two years
The first federal immigration ban was the 1803 Immigration Act, whose main proponents were enslavers seeking to block the entry of Black Caribbeans fleeing the Haitian Revolution
This pattern persisted for the next 150 years
In the mid-19th century, California state legislators levied a tax on foreign miners to keep nonwhite immigrants away from the gold mines
In 1882, Congress passed the Chinese Exclusion Act , which survived in different guises and iterations until 1943

And the 1924 Johnson-Reed Act established national-origins quotas that capped the total number of immigrants at 150,000 a year, while reserving 96 percent of those slots for European immigrants and 84 percent for those from northwestern Europe, according to Lytle Hernández

Senator David Reed, a Republican from Pennsylvania who co-authored the law, said, “We have closed the doors just in time to prevent our nordic population being overrun by lower races.” By 1940, Lytle Hernández writes, Europeans and Canadians, who at this point were all considered equally white, accounted for 94 percent of the foreign-born population living in the United States

Even after laws were liberalized and these numbers changed, members of both political parties tried to boost the proportion of white immigrants by prioritizing what the liberal Senator Ted Kennedy called the “old seed sources of our heritage.” This was all before the Trump administration made race-based immigration de facto American policy—most pointedly by deporting mainly nonwhite immigrants while welcoming white South Africans who claimed to be victims of a Black-led government
The author shows how the intrinsic racism of these moves is not accidental or incidental, but by design

She adds fresh insights as well by tracking the gradual concentration of immigration enforcement in the hands of the federal government, and by showing how fights over naturalization were entwined with debates over the treatment of Black people and Native Americans
And she reframes the immigration story as focusing on not only the people we let into the country, but also those we keep out

This complicates Americans’ conception of themselves as a nation of immigrants; we are also a nation that has excluded them. [ Read: Republicans vs. the Fourteenth Amendment ] Lytle Hernández is too good a historian to skip over more permissive periods, even when they fail to serve her argument

She calls the passage of the 1866 Civil Rights Act and the Fourteenth Amendment the “single-largest mass naturalization action in U.S. history,” because these laws “created more than four million new African American citizens.” When white settlers in the western U.S. challenged the birthright citizenship of Chinese Americans, the Supreme Court, in its 1898 ruling United States v

Wong Kim Ark , “unambiguously affirmed” that almost all children born in the United States were citizens. (The children of Native Americans, diplomats, and occupying troops in a hypothetical invasion were exceptions.) Nobody has conclusively counted the number of Americans born to undocumented immigrants who became citizens because of the Fourteenth Amendment, but the Pew Research Center has calculated that it has exceeded 100,000 a year since at least 1990
Barbara decision , the Supreme Court invalidated the president’s executive order limiting birthright citizenship and explicitly upheld the ruling in Wong Kim Ark
John Sauer, argued that the authors of the Fourteenth Amendment intended to extend birthright citizenship only to freed slaves and their children
But a majority of the justices found that the language of the amendment was plain and applied to almost every person born in the United States, no matter their race or heritage
As alarming as it was that three justices sided with Trump, the decision, like earlier rulings from the top court, undermines Lytle Hernández’s idea of a whites-only immigration regime
Often, the author downplays government action by the courts, Congress, or presidents that benefited nonwhite immigrants
As a result of the 1965 Immigration and Nationality Act , which ended national-origins quotas, the United States went from being 16 percent nonwhite to 40 percent nonwhite in 60 years
Lytle Hernández frames this accomplishment as the unintentional result of mistaken reassurances; President Lyndon B
Johnson, for one, announced that it was not “a revolutionary bill,” and would not change people’s daily lives

Insofar as it altered the nation’s ethnic makeup, restrictionists felt that it did change their lives—and ever since, they have considered it to be one of the worst pieces of legislation in American history

The 1965 act contained strong, explicitly anti-racist language: “No person shall receive any preference or priority or be discriminated against in the issuance of an immigrant visa because of his race, sex, nationality, place of birth, or place of residence.” Lytle Hernández quotes this passage, but then immediately points out that the law left in place measures that disproportionately affected Mexican immigrants

title: The Download: moon city problems and drone traffic controllers
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century
But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp
A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings
That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating
But the chief obstacle may be one of political will
Find out what stands in the way of a city on the moon . —Robin George Andrews This story is from the next issue of our print magazine

Subscribe now to get your hands on a copy as soon as it lands on Wednesday 21 October!   10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Brimstone and its one-stop process for making cleaner cement and critical minerals Brimstone is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026 , available exclusively to subscribers
Brimstone is a code-switching climate tech company for these polarized political times
The US startup is part green cement company, part critical mineral producer
During the Biden administration, its primary pitch was cement that generates about 60% fewer greenhouse-gas emissions
It achieves this by switching to silicate rocks instead of standard limestone, which releases carbon dioxide when heated
Under the Trump administration, however, the company is emphasizing another benefit of its process: the ability to extract valuable materials from those same rocks

Discover how it’s making strides on two industrial problems . —James Temple Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch , spanning everything from geothermal power plants to smart turbines and semi-solid-state cells

Job titles of the future: Delivery drone air traffic controller The moment Trevor Wischnewsky heard that drones were delivering pizza and sushi around his Texas neighborhood, his mind was made up. “It was super fascinating,” he says. “I just immediately wanted to be a part of it.” Wischnewsky is now an RPIC, or remote pilot in command, at a company called FlyTrex
An RPIC is like an air traffic controller

But instead of airplanes, they oversee fleets of drones that ferry cargo to homes and businesses Here’s what it takes to become a drone air traffic controller . —Eamon Whalen The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 An Anthropic AI model submitted a fake tip about an unsolved murder The tip was in a new group of rogue actions Anthropic disclosed. ( NYT $) + Police criticised the company for waiting nine days to report it after finding it. ( WSJ $) + Another model submitted real government forms. ( Quartz ) + The White House has made AI incident reporting mandatory. ( Axios ) + But who’s liable when AI agents go rogue? ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 Ukraine’s drone strikes have dealt a major blow to Russian AI Sunday’s attack shut down the third Yandex data centre hit in days. ( Reuters $) + The strikes have disrupted Russia’s AI, cloud services, and apps. ( Gizmodo ) + They followed Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centers. ( Ars Technica ) + Russian military satellites could disrupt Starlink. ( Reuters $) + Ukraine’s drone data is fueling a wild market. ( MIT Technology Review ) 3 Iranian ChatGPT users have planted AI-generated articles in news outlets About a dozen outlets ran roughly 100 articles by fake journalists. ( CNN ) + The articles criticised the Iran war’s effects on Americans. ( WP $) + AI has been used to turn the Iran conflict into theatre. ( MIT Technology Review ) 4 Tesla has renamed “Full Self-Driving” as “Assisted Driving” in Europe EU lawmakers said the old name was misleading.  ( TechCrunch ) + Tesla hopes the rebrand leads regulators to approve the feature. ( Wired $) + Back in the US, it plans to increase toxic emissions near a school. ( SFGate ) 5 A ransomware negotiator has been arrested amid a hacking crackdown The FBI suspects he was involved with a gang that recently claimed to have stolen data on the bureau’s employees. ( Reuters $) + AI is making online crimes easier. ( MIT Technology Review ) 6 Hollywood’s hottest villain right now is the tech billionaire Four new films feature dark depictions of Silicon Valley leaders. ( Axios $) + The real Mark Zuckerberg has also become a new character. ( NYT $) 7 A new experiment is testing the Amazon’s response to rising CO ₂ CO₂-releasing towers will simulate future atmospheric conditions. ( Nature ) + Is carbon removal in trouble? ( MIT Technology Review ) 8 The US hybrid boom has pushed some used car prices above new ones Buyers are paying a premium to skip the wait for new models. ( Wired $) 9 A new technology switches tattoos on and off with light It can make permanent ink invisible. ( New Scientist $) 10 Scientists spotted the most distant signal yet from the ancient universe It could help them understand how the universe has evolved. ( 404 Media ) Quote of the day “ Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI.”  —Microsoft’s president, Brad Smith, tells the BBC why AI urgently needs more regulations, including requiring firms to write “incident reports” and tell victims if the technology goes rogue

One more thing LINDA NYLIND / EYEVINE VIA REDUX Geoffrey Hinton tells us why he’s now scared of the tech he helped build Geoffrey Hinton is a pioneer of deep learning who helped develop some of the most important techniques at the heart of modern artificial intelligence, but after a decade at Google, he’s stepped down to focus on concerns he now has about AI
Hinton is now spending his time on what he describes as “more philosophical work.” And that will focus on the small but—to him—very real danger that AI will turn out to be a disaster

Here’s why he’s so worried . —Will Douglas Heaven We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .) + A doting blind cat has been following his owner everywhere like a little duckling. + Eigendrum lets you draw any shape and hear what it would sound like as a real drum. + Build your perfect background soundscape with Ambient Mixer , from rainy forests to cozy cafés. + Meet Momota, the polar bear cub who’s turning traffic cones into an unlikely fashion statement .

title: Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind
excerpt: You can be forgiven for experiencing déjà vu
body: You can be forgiven for experiencing déjà vu
Last time, it was the Soviet Union and the United States vying to be the first to plant some flags
Now it’s a sprint to the lunar surface between America and China—alongside a host of varyingly friendly and rival nations—plus a cornucopia of private spaceflight companies
And this time it looks like they’re getting ready to set up camp
There will be, the contenders say, bases on the moon, permanently inhabited castles under the stars
The notion of a moon base, fanciful as it might sound, isn’t new
But this year, under the leadership of Administrator Jared Isaacman, NASA has been flooding the zone with bold announcements

If all goes according to plan—a plan that will likely cost tens of billions of dollars to start—there will be drones , robotic landers, communication satellites , and a nuclear power plant ; there will be plant terrariums and moonquake sensors; there will be mechanized scouts exploring craters for water
Initial astronaut missions to the lunar surface, which the US is currently planning to start in 2028, will be focused on exploration and technological experimentation

But the idea is that we will—some time in the 2030s—get to a point where there will be habitation quarters for long-term stays, surrounded by a network of scientific research stations, resource mining and processing plants, and landing pads for spaceships. “It’s going to be an expanse,” says Carlos García-Galán, NASA’s moon base program manager—one that will add up to “hundreds of square miles.” The effort is undoubtedly being fueled by nationalistic competition
China has near-identical plans to build its own base on the moon
And being first matters, because the “victor” gets to define the terms
What is the moon, exactly? Is it a militarized outpost? Is it a manufacturing hub? Is it a wilderness to be studied and preserved? But there are also other reasons to go
Earth’s companion contains primeval rocks that hold clues to the formation of the entire solar system
The lunar surface, with virtually no atmosphere in the way, is an ideal place to put telescopes that could examine the most ancient epochs of the cosmos
The far side of the moon would be “a fantastic place to explore the further universe,” says Josef Aschbacher, the European Space Agency’s director general

And it’s way more energy efficient to launch rockets from the low-gravity lunar surface than it is from Earth, meaning sending astronauts—or robotic spacecraft—farther into the solar system will become much less difficult. “The moon is critical
It will be a stepping stone for going further—that means to Mars and beyond,” says Aschbacher
SELMAN DESIGN But if these bold visions are to become reality, there’s a daunting amount of work to be done
A sprawling moon base must be safe for its astronaut inhabitants—protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings
It also must be somewhat self-sustaining, so that it can weather changing political fortunes and not cost ruinous amounts of money to maintain
For that, we’ll need to find a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating—and ideally generating revenue

And we’ll need autonomous robots that can build, maintain, and expand the base even when their human masters aren’t present. “It’s almost like starting civilization from scratch,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales

Assuming we can overcome these starting challenges, decades from now—let’s say, by the year 2100—our initial moon bases could grow from barely visible structures into luminous cities, perhaps not too dissimilar from those dreamed up by authors and screenwriters the world over. “It’s like science fiction today that we really want to turn into a reality,” says García-Galán
Will anyone succeed? The moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp
In general, daytime temperatures can reach more than 250 °F; at night, they can plummet to less than –200 °F
Exposed to the vacuum of space, the surface is constantly showered in carcinogenic radiation and frequently hit by meteoroids
And its volcanic dust is sticky and corrosive, a destroyer of equipment and choker of lungs.  Sadly, the lunar south pole—the area NASA is targeting—is even harsher
NASA wants to build a base there because its permanently shadowed craters are thought to harbor caches of water ice, which would be more precious than gold
Purify it, and you can water crops and hydrate astronauts; split it into oxygen and hydrogen, and you have breathable air and rocket propellant
But the temperature in those craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe
On the surface outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night

But there is only so much money we can spend on safety. “What it comes down to is acceptable risk of death,” Philip Metzger , a spaceflight engineering researcher at the Florida Space Institute, said while pondering some of the dangers. “What can we reasonably survive without breaking the bank?” Temperature is one of the easiest problems to handle
Materials science has come a long way, and there are myriad metals, ceramics, plastics, compounds, and alloys that can resist wild temperature swings
Radiators keep things cool; heaters keep batteries from dying prematurely
Astronauts survive just fine too, with their fancy spacesuits—but that technology has proved itself only during brief excursions
It’s not yet clear how long this equipment could operate under such tempestuous conditions
The temperature in the moon’s south pole craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe
Outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night
Space radiation, which can wreak havoc on electronics and trigger a cancerous division of cells, is far more pernicious

title: The ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests
excerpt: In a research station in central Panama, you can walk through a century of forest time, watching scrubby plots of adolescent trees give way to cathedral-­like c
body: In a research station in central Panama, you can walk through a century of forest time, watching scrubby plots of adolescent trees give way to cathedral-­like canopies of mature growth
Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, oversees this sequence of plots across the Barro Colorado Nature Monument, some of which date as far back as the 19th century
Not one of the trees she surveys was planted by human hands

She maps, measures, and tracks each trunk that emerges, revealing how waves of tree life rise from bare earth.  Tropical forests like these are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land
As part of an international network of researchers, Dent is deciphering the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction
The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree

For over a decade, her research has built a body of evidence that such large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide
Few places are better to demonstrate this than Barro Colorado, a reserve covering the forested peninsulas and islands that formed when construction of the Panama Canal flooded the area in 1914

Under the management of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, generations of ecologists have amassed more than a century of records.  That means Dent can trace why some plots rebound after clear-cutting for farming and forestry while others falter

Fruit-eating animals—including spider monkeys, bats, and parrots—are responsible for planting more than 70% of trees in tropical forests, and Dent’s dataset can tell which built each patch of trees by depositing seeds in their nutrient-rich droppings
Many of these creatures worked together to plant a diverse 70-year-old patch whose canopy is approaching the stunning structure and richness of an ancient jungle

In contrast, a patch of similar age populated by narrow trunks of a single long-lived species, Gustavia superba , hints that tropical rodents called agoutis are more or less the sole animal architects behind this more homogeneous forest.  The data she collects helps write a playbook for when to let ecosystems regenerate and when to give them a helping hand

One 2024 estimate in Nature found that some 215 million hectares of forest worldwide (an area larger than Mexico) could regenerate naturally. “Tropical forests are underpinned by this massive network of interactions,” Dent says—interactions between life-forms like the fungi that help trees take up nutrients, as well as pollinators and seed-distributors

Supporting those relationships is key to growing forests that lock up carbon and help sustain local communities and wildlife.  Filling in the gaps Just over a decade ago, as the landmark Paris Agreement was being codified in 2015, forest recovery seized global attention as a solution to the climate crisis
Global leaders rallied behind plans to regrow a trillion trees , after the ecologist Thomas Crowther highlighted their potential to capture a decade’s worth of global carbon emissions

But the biggest question has lingered: How, exactly, do you regrow two trees for every star in the Milky Way? While startups have proposed seed-spraying drones and nutrient-coated seed bombs , Dent has spent two decades studying what happens when we let forests rebuild themselves
As a PhD student around the turn of the millennium, she researched old-growth forests in northern Borneo but felt hopeless watching entire landscapes felled for palm oil plantations
Rather than despair, she turned to restoration

Then, as a postdoc in 2005, she joined Panama’s Prorena, a joint initiative between the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute and the Yale School of Forestry and Environmental Studies, which aimed at determining how best to establish diverse native forests on clear-cut land
Back then, secondary forests—ones that grow naturally after the original forest was lost—had been “a bit of a niche research area,” Dent says
But as farming and human infrastructure have driven deforestation, resurgent forests now account for some 70% of all tropical canopies
Prorena initially followed the usual playbook of transplanting nursery trees to rangelands, but Dent began to question whether planting was necessary
In 2009, she published an encouraging paper showing that animal populations rebound quickly as forests naturally regrow
In 2010, she began working in Barro Colorado on the plots established by the pioneering American ecologist Julie Denslow

In 1994, Denslow identified plots that had been regenerating naturally for 20 to 100 years, and Dent would add younger ones to continue the sequence.  The site provides not just general data on forest regrowth but in-depth demographic information over time, says Robin Chazdon, a professor emeritus of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Connecticut who collaborated with Denslow when she established the plots. “It tells you more about the actual processes that are happening in the site,” she says.  For example, previous research had shown that fast-growing “pioneer trees,” the first to thrive in the damaged land, are eventually overtaken by larger carbon-storing trees
Dent’s research helped fill in gaps about the mechanics of how this happens—or doesn’t happen—in individual cases
In the Gustavia -dominated patch, for instance, stubborn grasses planted by cattle ranchers smothered most other trees before they could take root

These trees can hang around, crowding out the light, for 150 years, blocking the second wave of large-trunked trees.  To plant or not to plant Dent found herself well placed for the massive influx of interest in reforestation that began in 2015
She’d already become a principal investigator for 2ndFor, an international research network aiming to learn how best to manage secondary forests

Using data gathered from the Barro Colorado plots, the team authored a 2016 paper in Nature showing that a hectare of naturally regenerated secondary forest can capture 11 times as much carbon each year as an old-growth one, with young trees absorbing it quickly as they compete to grow toward the sun

Then, in a 2022 study published by the Royal Society, Dent and colleagues showed that locations such as Barro Colorado are among the best-case scenarios for what can be achieved without planting a single seed
Clearings are often surrounded by lush environments filled with birds, bats, and other animals, all of which help tree cover regain old-growth levels of richness and abundance within a few decades

Using data from Panama and Brazil, Dent published a follow-up in 2024 showing that plots with as little as 35% of tree cover can regenerate as forest.  “Having these long-term mapped forest plots is really valuable,” says Liza Comita, a professor of tropical forest ecology at Yale University, who is collaborating with Dent on projects that translate her findings into action. “It provides this really nice research infrastructure where you can build projects on top of that.”  In Panama, Dent works with nonprofits and carbon-crediting schemes to fast-track recovery
They’ve mapped corridors to reconnect forest fragments and made plans to reintroduce animals in “silent forests” that have lost much of their wildlife
They’re also working to replant tree species that can accelerate growth—what Comita calls assisted natural regeneration
Leaving plots alone may seem like the simpler option, but it can’t be done everywhere, says Dent
Many sites are too degraded.  Clearings are often surrounded by lush environments filled with birds, bats, and other animals, all of which helps tree cover regain old-growth ­levels of richness
The two are working with the London-based carbon-crediting startup Ponterra to develop solutions for a region of southern Panama where remnant forests line the edges of abandoned ranches
Such sites almost always need some intervention, Comita explains
Many demand hands-on actions, such as enrichment planting.  Today, the questions projects like Ponterra are asking are closer to her own research, says Dent

title: California is taking a beating from an unusually destructive 2026 Pacific hurricane season
url:
<title>California is taking a beating from an unusually destructive 2026 Pacific hurricane season</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765648/original/file-20261012-50-6zix9r.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=79%2C0%2C7761%2C5174&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Waves crash into damaged homes in Long Beach, Calif., amid high surf generated by Tropical Storm Rachel on Oct. 11, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/in-an-aerial-view-pacific-ocean-waves-wash-into-damaged-news-photo/2299702764?phrase=california%20storm&amp;adppopup=true">Mario Tama/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>California isn’t a place most Americans associate with tropical weather, but it’s taking a beating in 2026 from one of the most active eastern Pacific hurricane seasons in modern history.</p>

<p>For the second time ever, national forecasters issued <a href="https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2026/ep18/ep182026.public.050.shtml">a tropical storm watch for Southern California</a> as Tropical Storm Rachel headed toward the region, bringing high tides, coastal flooding and drenching rain from Oct. 9-11. The first tropical storm watch was issued just <a href="https://theconversation.com/tropical-storm-hilary-pounds-southern-california-with-heavy-rain-flash-flooding-211869">three years earlier</a>, for Hurricane Hilary.</p>

<p>The U.S. occasionally sees heavy rain from the remnants of Pacific storms that pass over Mexico and travel into the U.S. Southwest. But the 2026 season has been different. Three <a href="https://theconversation.com/another-hurricane-just-sideswiped-hawaii-why-the-islands-usual-force-field-seems-to-be-down-in-2026-291524">hurricanes deluged Hawaii</a> as they passed close to the islands, a rare event for that state. And in September, <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/alisondurkee/2026/09/07/hurricane-marie-brings-ten-foot-waves-and-flooding-to-southern-california-photos/">Hurricane Marie churned up big waves</a> that damaged oceanfront homes near Los Angeles before veering away from the coast. </p>

<p>Rachel <a href="https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2026/ep18/ep182026.discus.056.shtml">weakened to an extratropical cyclone</a> before its landfall in Baja California, but it brought high waves to Southern California that <a href="https://ktla.com/news/local-news/long-beach-assessing-damages-from-tropical-storm-rachel-threat-of-powerful-waves-still-not-over/">damaged more coastal homes</a> and flooded streets. Its rainfall drenched communities from San Diego to the desert Southwest and even triggered <a href="https://www.ktnv.com/news/video-rain-from-tropical-storm-rachel-causes-flooding-across-las-vegas-valley">flooding in Las Vegas</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765665/original/file-20261012-50-d21llr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Flooded streets in a coastal town." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765665/original/file-20261012-50-d21llr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765665/original/file-20261012-50-d21llr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=403&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765665/original/file-20261012-50-d21llr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=403&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765665/original/file-20261012-50-d21llr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=403&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765665/original/file-20261012-50-d21llr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=506&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765665/original/file-20261012-50-d21llr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=506&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765665/original/file-20261012-50-d21llr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=506&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>

<p><a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=5uEy_XoAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">I study Pacific hurricanes</a>. While tropical storm impacts to California are unusual, they aren’t unprecedented. El Niño raises the risks.</p>

<h2>California’s history with tropical storms</h2>

<p>Historically, Southern California has seen a few direct hits from tropical storms and numerous cases of damage from systems that remained offshore.</p>

<p>To find the earliest known storm there, we <a href="https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/bams/85/11/bams-85-11-1689.pdf">have to travel back all the way to 1858</a>, when a Category 1 hurricane, simply known as the 1858 San Diego Hurricane, brushed the coast of San Diego County and brought tropical-storm-force winds to the region. San Diego of the 1850s had a fraction of the population it has today, but the storm still caused significant damage. </p>





<p>While weaker than the 1858 hurricane, the only tropical storm known to have made landfall on the California coast was a <a href="https://www.weather.gov/media/wrh/online_publications/TMs/TM-197.pdf">1939 tropical storm that hit Long Beach</a>, in Los Angeles County. It brought tropical-storm-force winds across a large swath of Southern California, <a href="https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2019-08-21/hurricanes-here-the-cordonazo-that-lashed-los-angeles">along with over 4 inches of rain in some areas</a>. </p>

<p>That storm was a surprise, and the United States Weather Bureau – the precursor to the modern National Weather Service – opened a Southern California office in 1940 in response. A 2004 research paper hypothesized that if a similar storm hit the region in the mid-2000s, it would have likely caused over US$200 million in damage to the region.</p>

<p>While a few other tropical storms in the 1970s came close to a landfall in California, all weakened or changed course, avoiding a direct hit. This includes the <a href="https://theconversation.com/tropical-storm-hilary-pounds-southern-california-with-heavy-rain-flash-flooding-211869">remnants of Hurricane Hilary</a> in 2023 that were still strong enough to cause widespread flooding in Southern California and dump <a href="https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/EP092023_Hilary.pdf">10 inches of rain in the mountains</a>.</p>

<p>A handful of additional systems that made landfall in Baja California or stayed offshore have brought tropical-storm-force winds to the state, including <a href="https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/EP161997_Nora.pdf">Hurricane Nora in 1997</a>. </p>

<p>In addition, multiple recent storms over the open ocean have generated swells that damaged port and pier infrastructure in the region, including <a href="https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/EP132014_Marie.pdf">hurricanes Marie in 2024</a>, <a href="https://ktla.com/news/local-news/hurricane-narda-causing-high-surf-at-southern-california-beaches/">Narda in 2025</a> and <a href="https://www.youtube.com/shorts/CIE_evQTzqs">another Marie in 2026</a>. </p>

<h2>El Niño raises California’s storm risk</h2>

<p>Several environmental factors increase the probability of tropical storms making an approach to Southern California.</p>

<p>The most notable is El Niño. This <a href="https://youtu.be/WPA-KpldDVc?si=KLh2d0eAq07Lih-0">natural climate pattern</a>, defined by unusually warm water in the eastern tropical Pacific, <a href="https://theconversation.com/2026s-el-nino-is-shaping-up-to-be-a-doozy-its-already-affecting-global-shipping-fish-behavior-and-heat-291490">increases the frequency of storms</a> in the eastern North Pacific. That’s because warmer than normal sea surface temperatures in the region are necessary to support the formation and development of these storms.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765630/original/file-20261012-50-a5bsi2.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A map shows storm tracks, including Rachel crossing the Baja Peninsula and entering California." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765630/original/file-20261012-50-a5bsi2.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765630/original/file-20261012-50-a5bsi2.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=324&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765630/original/file-20261012-50-a5bsi2.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=324&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765630/original/file-20261012-50-a5bsi2.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=324&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765630/original/file-20261012-50-a5bsi2.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=408&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765630/original/file-20261012-50-a5bsi2.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=408&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765630/original/file-20261012-50-a5bsi2.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=408&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Storm tracks during an exceptionally active eastern Pacific hurricane season in 2026 show the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel, No. 18, crossing into California.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/index.php?basin=epac">NOAA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Even during El Niño years, the waters off the coast of Southern California and northern Baja California are <a href="https://www.ospo.noaa.gov/products/ocean/sst/contour/">typically too cool</a> to <a href="https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/ocean-fact/hurricanes/">support hurricanes</a>. Still, storms moving fast enough or with enough support from upper-level winds can survive these slightly cooler temperatures, allowing the system to make an approach toward California.</p>

<p>When Tropical Storm Rachel began its approach toward Southern California on Oct. 9, the <a href="https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2026/ep18/ep182026.discus.051.shtml">National Hurricane Center noted</a> that the sea surface temperatures were anomalously warm off the coast of Baja California and played a role in its potential to remain a tropical cyclone as it approached the coast.</p>

<h2>The big storm problem: Rain</h2>

<p>Like most eastern Pacific tropical storms and hurricanes, the primary effect on California from these systems is rainfall.</p>

<p>Most of Southern California is arid and rarely receives rainfall during summer and early fall. Early reports showed <a href="https://forecast.weather.gov/product.php?site=sgx&amp;issuedby=SGX&amp;product=RRM">Rachel dumped upward of 6 inches of rain</a> in parts of Southern California, including over 1 inch at San Diego International Airport in one weekend. That inch of rain in San Diego is double the typical October precipitation there.</p>

<p>While those amounts may seem minuscule compared to what typically comes with a tropical storm or hurricane landfall in places like Florida, they can cause flash flooding in the normally dry Southwest. The National Hurricane Center <a href="https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2026/ep18/ep182026.public.053.shtml">warned of flash flooding</a> in California and other parts of the Southwest before Rachel’s landfall.</p>

<p>Unique cases like Rachel show that Mother Nature can always go against conventional wisdom, and, given enough time and the right conditions, potentially destructive things can happen.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294207/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
