<title>Hooked on tuna: People have been harvesting these ocean predators for 44,000 years</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765306/original/file-20261009-50-7ar5dc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5184%2C3456&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">For millennia, people have found ways to locate, catch and share tunas.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/bluefin-tuna-thunnus-thynnus-saltwater-fish-royalty-free-image/1334276621">LUNAMARINA/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>From a humble mayonnaise-laden sandwich to an expensive piece of sashimi, tuna is a prized source of food for people around the world. Once an inexpensive, easily shipped canned protein source, today’s bluefin tunas can fetch <a href="https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/see-the-record-breaking-bluefin-tuna-the-size-of-a-grizzly-bear-that-sold-for-3-2-million-at-a-tokyo-fish-market-180987988/">millions of dollars at auction</a>. Millions of tons of tuna are harvested every year, supporting a global industry worth around <a href="https://www.iss-foundation.org/about-issf/what-we-publish/issf-documents/issf-2026-01-status-of-the-world-fisheries-for-tuna-january-2026/">US$40 billion annually</a>.</p>

<p>But tunas are more than just the pink flesh found in cans and sushi, and humanity’s story with these fish goes back further than you might expect.</p>

<p>As <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=fLtI9XkAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">a biologist</a> and an <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=i0MgN2EAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">archaeologist</a> interested in long-term human-environment interactions, we wanted to investigate the deep record of people’s relationship with tunas.</p>

<p>We drew on the expertise of 18 leading researchers worldwide and studied a variety of sources, from the skeletal remains of tunas in archaeological sites to ancient rock art, paintings on frescos and vases, written historical records and ethnographic accounts from Indigenous communities. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2512066123">This data helped us understand</a> where, when and why people caught tunas, and what cultural and environmental forces shaped these early fisheries. In turn, this provided new insights into how past harvests compare with the millions of tons caught today.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763770/original/file-20261004-50-n4bjms.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3072%2C1728&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="School of dark silvery fish swimming together against deep blue water" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763770/original/file-20261004-50-n4bjms.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3072%2C1728&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763770/original/file-20261004-50-n4bjms.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763770/original/file-20261004-50-n4bjms.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763770/original/file-20261004-50-n4bjms.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763770/original/file-20261004-50-n4bjms.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763770/original/file-20261004-50-n4bjms.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763770/original/file-20261004-50-n4bjms.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Tunas travel in schools that can include thousands of individual fish.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/bluefin-tuna-in-net-royalty-free-image/95662678">DeepAqua/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>An apex predator of the ocean</h2>

<p>“Tuna” is a common name given to a group of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1546-5098(01)19002-3">15 fish species</a>. The major market species include eight “true tunas” in genus <em>Thunnus</em> along with skipjack tuna (<em>Katsuwonus pelamis</em>).</p>

<p>Tunas are among the largest predators in the open ocean, with some species reaching almost <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11160-012-9284-4">10 feet (over 3 meters) in length and living for over 40 years</a>. Tuna are champion swimmers; Pacific bluefin tuna can migrate 5,000 miles (8,000 kilometers) across the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pocean.2018.02.010">northern Pacific in a matter of months</a>.</p>

<p>Tuna are also ecologically important apex predators and serve as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abj0211">sentinels of ocean health</a>. However, most scientific research has focused on the past 75 years, with assessments of the health of tuna populations <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abj0211">benchmarked against the year 1950</a>. The focus on recent decades raises a variety of questions about the deeper history of fishing for tuna prior to the past century.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765391/original/file-20261011-50-twtn7f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Three people stand at the side of a cave with a dirt floor" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765391/original/file-20261011-50-twtn7f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765391/original/file-20261011-50-twtn7f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765391/original/file-20261011-50-twtn7f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765391/original/file-20261011-50-twtn7f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765391/original/file-20261011-50-twtn7f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765391/original/file-20261011-50-twtn7f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765391/original/file-20261011-50-twtn7f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Archaeologists have found the earliest tuna bones harvested by people in Jerimalai Cave in East Timor.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Sue O’Connor</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>A deep and dynamic history</h2>

<p>The oldest definitive evidence of tuna fishing, in the form of skeletal remains of what were likely skipjack tuna, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1207703">comes from East Timor</a> in southeast Asia about <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s12520-019-00840-5">44,000 years ago</a>. Likely aided by deepwater channels that brought tunas close to shore, this early example of tuna fishing is somewhat unusual – most areas of the world don’t contain evidence of tuna fishing until 10,000 years ago or more recently. </p>

<p>Ancient fishers in Japan and Korea, for instance, captured tunas beginning at least 7,000 years ago, with a rich culinary tradition and large-scale harvests that trace their way to the present day love for these fishes in the region. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762370/original/file-20260925-60-9hsqix.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Scene with water on the top, land on the bottom, with people pulling nets that are penning in fish closer to land" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762370/original/file-20260925-60-9hsqix.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762370/original/file-20260925-60-9hsqix.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=212&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762370/original/file-20260925-60-9hsqix.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=212&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762370/original/file-20260925-60-9hsqix.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=212&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762370/original/file-20260925-60-9hsqix.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=266&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762370/original/file-20260925-60-9hsqix.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=266&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762370/original/file-20260925-60-9hsqix.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=266&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A 13th-century engraving shows tuna traps at Zahara de los Atunes, Spain, where fishers would tighten the net and pull the fish toward shore.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Fundación Casa Medina Sidonia</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The northeastern Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea are home to one of the world’s oldest and most important tuna fisheries, focused on Atlantic bluefin tuna. A few ancient tuna bones found in a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4419-8219-3_10">Neanderthal site in Gibraltar dating to around 26,000 years</a> ago may have been obtained by Neanderthals scavenging. However, by 9,000 to 11,000 years ago, thousands of tuna bones were deposited in Greece in a cave overlooking Kiladha Bay. The number of sites across Europe with tuna remains increases rapidly in the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/icesjms/fsab261">archaeological record after about 8,000 years ago</a>.</p>

<p>These early fishers used a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/2241-5793-21-2">variety of methods to catch tuna</a>, including hook and line, harpoons, and traps or nets. They often took advantage of topographic features where fish could be driven close to shore. This tuna fishing is captured in written records, paintings and other art, showing the cultural importance of these fish to ancient European societies. The ancient Greeks deemed tuna worthy of sacrifice to the gods and used them as <a href="https://doi.org/10.5252/anthropozoologica2021v56a2">offerings to Poseidon</a>.</p>

<p>By 3,000 years ago, a commercial Atlantic bluefin tuna fishery had formed in the Mediterranean, with large-scale trade and specialized nets and traps. By the 16th and 17th centuries, people may have caught <a href="https://www.iccat.int/Documents/CVSP/CV073_2017/n_6/CV073062074.pdf">tens of thousands of tons annually</a>. This fishery was made possible by the predictable <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/icesjms/fsab261">migration patterns of Atlantic bluefin and coastal access to tunas</a> – no dangerous oceanic voyages necessary.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762372/original/file-20260925-50-20uf2n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Dirty bone, round on one edge, held by hands" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762372/original/file-20260925-50-20uf2n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762372/original/file-20260925-50-20uf2n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762372/original/file-20260925-50-20uf2n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762372/original/file-20260925-50-20uf2n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762372/original/file-20260925-50-20uf2n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762372/original/file-20260925-50-20uf2n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762372/original/file-20260925-50-20uf2n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A Pacific bluefin tuna bone from an archaeological site on Vancouver Island.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Iain McKechnie</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>For over 5,000 years, Indigenous people on North America’s northwest coast, particularly in Nuu-chah-nulth territory, had an <a href="https://spo.nmfs.noaa.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-content/1997/951/crockford.pdf">important and complex fishery for Pacific bluefin tuna</a>.</p>

<p>Ethnographic accounts from native elders describe how during unique warm-water events in late summer, people voyaged out at night into the fjords, aided by natural bioluminescent plankton. With spotters overlooking the fjords and communicating from land, fishers set fires in canoes to lure tuna close enough to harpoon. People would spear these massive fish, some perhaps more than 6 feet (2 meters) in length and weighing 640 pounds (290 kilograms). Bluefin tuna vertebrae have been found in <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/faf.70024">23 regional archaeological sites</a>.</p>

<p>In Southern California, people also captured tunas, particularly around Santa Catalina Island, where Indigenous fishers caught Pacific bluefin, yellowfin, albacore and skipjack tunas for <a href="https://escholarship.org/uc/item/96394460">6,000 years, leaving the fishes’ skeletal remains</a> in regional archaeological sites.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765084/original/file-20261008-50-727giw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="black and white photo of men on both sides of a chute with large fish between them" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765084/original/file-20261008-50-727giw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765084/original/file-20261008-50-727giw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=744&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765084/original/file-20261008-50-727giw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=744&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765084/original/file-20261008-50-727giw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=744&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765084/original/file-20261008-50-727giw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=934&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765084/original/file-20261008-50-727giw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=934&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765084/original/file-20261008-50-727giw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=934&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Workers at a Starkist tuna cannery in 1953 in California.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/workers-at-a-fish-cannery-tuna-fish-comes-down-a-chute-at-news-photo/955062040">Charles E. Rotkin/Corbis/VCG via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>However, it wasn’t until the 19th and 20th centuries that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/faf.70024">commercial and sport fisheries</a> for tuna developed in the area. Tuna experienced a meteoric rise in popularity during World War I and World War II. Often centered around canneries in Los Angeles and San Diego, Southern California commercial and industrial tuna fisheries benefited from Japanese and Portuguese immigrant fishing communities, which helped spawn a global industry for tuna.</p>

<h2>Emergence of oceanic exploitation</h2>

<p>Tuna consumption by people is obviously nothing new. But how has the scale of tuna harvest changed through time?</p>

<p>Using the quantity of tuna bones present in archaeological sites as a rough metric, we found that even the largest of these ancient fisheries – those in the Mediterranean – likely only removed thousands of tonnes of tuna over millennia, which pales in comparison to the millions of tons of tuna now removed from the oceans every year.</p>

<p>This contrast brings up important questions: What are the consequences of oceanic exploitation exploding over such a relatively short period of time? How can people sustainably manage tuna populations? There are no easy answers, and three of the commercially important tuna species – southern bluefin, Pacific bluefin and bigeye tuna – <a href="https://www.iucnredlist.org/search?query=thunnus&amp;searchType=species">remain endangered, vulnerable or near threatened</a>. However, in several regions a combination of effective governance, monitoring and harvest controls have <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abj0211">stabilized tuna populations</a> even with intensive harvests. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765086/original/file-20261008-50-6j1o01.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Water color painting of a blue fish with Japanese writing" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765086/original/file-20261008-50-6j1o01.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765086/original/file-20261008-50-6j1o01.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=410&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765086/original/file-20261008-50-6j1o01.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=410&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765086/original/file-20261008-50-6j1o01.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=410&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765086/original/file-20261008-50-6j1o01.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=515&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765086/original/file-20261008-50-6j1o01.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=515&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765086/original/file-20261008-50-6j1o01.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=515&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">People have shared a long relationship with tuna, not just by harvesting them but also depicting them in art.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/bonito-and-saxifrage-from-an-untitled-series-of-fish-circa-news-photo/1365712579">Heritage Art/Heritage Images/Hulton Archive via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2512066123">deep history of tuna fishing</a> also highlights the human capacity for innovation. For more than 44,000 years, people have found ways to locate, catch and share tunas. That same capacity, channeled into international cooperation and science-based management, may help maintain global tuna stocks at sustainable levels – even if they’ll likely never again reach precommercial fishing levels of abundance.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292428/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>300 glaciers have disappeared from the American West since the mid-20th century – the survivors have a few things in common</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765315/original/file-20261009-60-q7ntv7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=1295%2C937%2C4305%2C2870&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Scientists take measurements on Sperry Glacier, in Glacier National Park, Montana.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.usgs.gov/media/images/researchers-sperry-glacier">USGS</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>From an airplane, most of the glaciers of the Rocky Mountain West look like small patches of white nestled into rugged landscape where the topography folds. The white is the snow cover, and lower down you can see the gray-blue bare ice.</p>

<p>In the middle of the 20th century, over 1,450 glaciers could be found in the contiguous U.S. Together, they covered 217 square miles (562 square kilometers) in six western states. Today, a comprehensive review my colleagues and I just published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences shows their <a href="https://www.pnas.org/cgi/doi/10.1073/pnas.2600941123">total area has shrunk by 35%</a> and they are still shrinking, perhaps faster.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765609/original/file-20261012-50-8z67ag.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Several glaciers nestled in shaded areas of high mountains." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765609/original/file-20261012-50-8z67ag.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765609/original/file-20261012-50-8z67ag.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=429&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765609/original/file-20261012-50-8z67ag.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=429&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765609/original/file-20261012-50-8z67ag.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=429&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765609/original/file-20261012-50-8z67ag.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=539&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765609/original/file-20261012-50-8z67ag.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=539&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765609/original/file-20261012-50-8z67ag.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=539&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Andrew Fountain took photos of glaciers in the Wind River Range in Wyoming while flying over the region in early October 2026. Most are located in protective niches.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Andrew Fountain</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>A little more than <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2600941123">300 glaciers have disappeared</a>, way more than I had anticipated.</p>

<p>Those that survive reflect just how vulnerable mountain glaciers have become as <a href="https://climate.copernicus.eu/climate-indicators/temperature">global temperatures rise</a>. Where glaciers <a href="https://www.nps.gov/features/romo/feat0001/GlcBasics.html">once covered large expanses</a> of the western mountains thousands of years ago, most of the <a href="https://nsidc.org/data/glacier_photo/">remaining glaciers in the Rockies and Sierra Nevada are small</a> and found in topographically protected places.</p>

<h2>Where US glaciers are disappearing fastest</h2>

<p>When people think of glaciers, they often picture huge ice streams with icebergs calving off the front, <a href="https://library.alaska.gov/asp/alaska_glaciers.HTML">like you’ll find in Alaska</a> or Greenland. In the Lower 48 states, with the exception of a few large glaciers in Washington, they’re much smaller.</p>

<p>We found that the average glacier area is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2600941123">about one-tenth of a square mile</a> (about a quarter of a square kilometer) in size. The area of the largest glacier, found on Washington’s Mount Rainier, is about 4.3 square miles (11.24 square kilometers).</p>

<p><iframe id="67wK3" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/67wK3/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Volume change in Mountain West glaciers"></iframe></p>

<p>I was surprised to find that glaciers in the Rocky Mountains – those in Colorado, Montana and Wyoming and in the Sierra Nevada of California – subsist because of their unique position on the landscape, which somewhat insulates them from the otherwise less-favorable regional climate.</p>

<p>The surviving Rocky Mountain glaciers inhabit shaded niches less exposed to direct sunshine and gain additional snow from avalanches. If these glaciers were exposed to more sun and less snow accumulation, they likely wouldn’t exit at all.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765311/original/file-20261009-50-wfwc8r.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Two images of the same view, with a large glacier in 1910 and only a sliver left in the shade in 2007." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765311/original/file-20261009-50-wfwc8r.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765311/original/file-20261009-50-wfwc8r.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=716&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765311/original/file-20261009-50-wfwc8r.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=716&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765311/original/file-20261009-50-wfwc8r.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=716&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765311/original/file-20261009-50-wfwc8r.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=900&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765311/original/file-20261009-50-wfwc8r.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=900&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765311/original/file-20261009-50-wfwc8r.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=900&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Two images of Montana’s Boulder Glacier, from 1910 and 2007, show how the ice in shaded areas survived longer.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.usgs.gov/media/images/boulder-glacier-1910-and-2007">USGS</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>We found the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2600941123">fastest-thinning</a> glaciers are in the <a href="https://www.umt.edu/this-is-montana/columns/stories/absaroka-beartooth-mountains.php">Beartooth-Absaroka Mountains</a> of the Rockies in southern Montana, which are losing about 1.5 feet (about half a meter) of ice thickness per year.</p>

<p>It’s a different story in Washington, where the glaciers on Mount Rainier and Mount Baker are much larger, have cooler summers and get a lot more snowfall. Although they too are shrinking, they do so at a much slower rate, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2600941123">about half a foot of ice</a> thickness per year. The glacier area on Mount Rainier alone is greater than the total sum in all the other states. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765608/original/file-20261012-50-xifo6o.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Three images of glaciers" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765608/original/file-20261012-50-xifo6o.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765608/original/file-20261012-50-xifo6o.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=323&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765608/original/file-20261012-50-xifo6o.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=323&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765608/original/file-20261012-50-xifo6o.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=323&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765608/original/file-20261012-50-xifo6o.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=406&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765608/original/file-20261012-50-xifo6o.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=406&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765608/original/file-20261012-50-xifo6o.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=406&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In Washington, generally speaking, the higher you go, the less glacier loss you find. That makes sense; it’s cooler at higher elevations. But in the Rocky Mountain region there is no similar trend, suggesting the survivors are niche glaciers that depend on local topographic benefits.</p>

<h2>What’s ahead</h2>

<p>In a study a few years ago, colleagues and I modeled the glaciers on Washington’s Olympic Peninsula and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1029/2022JF006670">found most would disappear by 2070</a> under current climate trends. That indicates that glaciers elsewhere are probably not far behind.</p>

<p>The Olympics are vulnerable because they’re close to the Pacific Ocean at somewhat lower elevation. The other Washington glaciers, particularly on Mount Rainier and Mount Baker, will likely survive past 2100, but how much longer is an open question.</p>



<p>That raises a few concerns. </p>

<p>The principal importance of the glaciers is to <a href="https://www.usgs.gov/news/meltwater-characteristics-western-mountain-glaciers-and-rock-glaciers">provide water to high alpine ecosystems</a>. The glaciers partially melt in late summer, providing cool water for cold-adapted fish and other stream life. They provide a water supply that’s otherwise absent in the dry late summer, after the seasonal snow disappears, when the region doesn’t get a lot of rain.</p>

<p>While the glaciers of the Rockies are primarily important for ecosystems at this point, those in Washington also <a href="https://www.seattle.gov/city-light/environment/climate-change-response/glaciers">contribute to hydropower production</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765330/original/file-20261009-50-d7lz7k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A glacier, glacial lake and debris flow image, annotated." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765330/original/file-20261009-50-d7lz7k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765330/original/file-20261009-50-d7lz7k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765330/original/file-20261009-50-d7lz7k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765330/original/file-20261009-50-d7lz7k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765330/original/file-20261009-50-d7lz7k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765330/original/file-20261009-50-d7lz7k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765330/original/file-20261009-50-d7lz7k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">When water builds up behind rock moraines created by glaciers, it can break through and cause large debris flows down the mountain. This photo shows a debris flow from the White River Glacier on Mount Hood in Oregon.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.usgs.gov/media/images/mount-hood-showing-white-river-glacier-and-location-debris-flow">William Scott/USGS</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>An important hazard is also associated with the glaciers on the steep-sided volcanoes of the Cascade Range, which stretches from California to Washington. The moraines formed by these glaciers are large, partly due to the highly erodible volcanic rock beneath the ice. Moving ice deposits eroded rocks, forming aprons at their lower ends. As the glaciers retreat, they leave the accumulated rocks behind as steep-sided moraines that are no longer buttressed by the ice.</p>

<p>High water flows from rain or glacier melt can undercut the moraines, triggering landslides and creating debris flows that go rocketing down the mountains. This <a href="https://www.nps.gov/articles/debris-flows.htm">happened in 2006 on Mount Hood and Mount Rainier</a> and closed a number of highways. We’ll see that happen more often as the glaciers retreat. </p>

<p>The shrinking and eventual loss of all of these glaciers will affect ecosystems across the West, as well as waterways humans and wildlife rely on.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294084/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>What colleges and universities need from donors to thrive</title>

Harvard was the school&#39;s first big donor.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/cambridge-ma-graduates-pass-the-john-harvard-statue-during-news-photo/2217074228?adppopup=true">Craig F. Walker/The Boston Globe via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>In 1638, <a href="https://askarc.hul.harvard.edu/faq/326814">John Harvard</a>, an English-born Puritan minister and teacher in the Massachusetts Bay Colony, bequeathed 400 books and half his £779 estate, today equivalent to roughly US$2 million, to the college that would be renamed in his honor after his death. </p>

<p>In addition to launching America’s oldest university, Harvard’s donation began a tradition of philanthropy for U.S. colleges and universities that has continued ever since. Today, philanthropy is an important source of higher education funding that covers an average of <a href="https://www.highereddive.com/news/charitable-giving-colleges-fy-2024-case/743015/">10% of college and university budgets</a>. </p>

<p><a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&amp;user=az6-_xcAAAAJ">Based on our</a> decades of <a href="https://philanthropy.indianapolis.iu.edu/people-directory/plater-william.html">experience as scholars</a>, academic administrators and <a href="https://philanthropy.indianapolis.iu.edu/people-directory/shaker-genevieve.html">school fundraisers</a>, we believe that donors – and not just big ones – are especially important to colleges and universities in tough times. </p>

<h2>In the crosshairs</h2>

<p>Since January 2025, the Trump administration has targeted colleges and universities with <a href="https://www.americanprogress.org/article/mapping-federal-funding-cuts-to-us-colleges-and-universities/">research funding cuts</a>, <a href="https://indianacapitalchronicle.com/2025/05/16/repub/what-to-know-about-the-u-s-house-gops-student-loan-overhaul/">student financial aid caps</a> and new restrictions on how <a href="https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov/final-rule-establishing-a-fixed-time-period-of-admission-and-an-extension-of-stay-procedure-quick">long international students can stay in the United States</a>. </p>

<p>University endowments have been in the crosshairs since the first Trump administration’s <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R44293">2017 tax reform package</a>. The big 2025 tax-and-spending package Trump signed raised <a href="https://taxpolicycenter.org/briefs/congress-has-increased-tax-college-and-university-endowments-how-should-we-think-about">the taxes on some schools’ endowments</a>. A rule the Trump administration proposed in September 2026 would threaten <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-the-trump-administrations-bid-to-end-diversity-efforts-at-nonprofit-schools-is-likely-to-get-tied-up-in-court-291338">private schools’ tax-exempt status</a> if any of their programs use race-based criteria. </p>

<p>There are demographic problems too. Fewer students are choosing to go to college, and the <a href="https://www.npr.org/2025/01/08/nx-s1-5246200/demographic-cliff-fewer-college-students-mean-fewer-graduates">number of high school graduates who could attend</a> is falling due to a <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data-visualization/natality-trends/index.htm">declining birthrate</a>.</p>

<p>Although colleges and universities are providing <a href="https://research.collegeboard.org/media/pdf/Trends-in-College-Pricing-and-Student-Aid-2025-final_1.pdf">more financial aid than ever</a>, students and their families are still struggling to <a href="https://www.highereddive.com/news/college-costs-for-families-up-10-from-last-year-poll-finds/827623/">pay for college</a>. </p>

<p>Some schools are being forced to close their doors. <a href="https://www.insidehighered.com/news/business/mergers-collaboration/2025/12/18/colleges-couldnt-survive-2025">Sixteen colleges shut down in 2025 alone</a>, including Indiana’s only predominantly Black college, Martin University, and ecologically focused Sterling College in Vermont.</p>

<p>And at least <a href="https://www.bestcolleges.com/research/closed-colleges-list-statistics-major-closures/">40 colleges have been acquired</a> by other schools since 2020, including <a href="https://news.northeastern.edu/marymount-manhattan-college-merger-faq/">Marymount Manhattan College</a> and <a href="https://news.northeastern.edu/2022/06/30/northeastern-mills-merger/">Mills College</a>, which are now part of Northeastern University’s global network. </p>

            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760314/original/file-20260916-50-clcl68.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A 'dear students' sticky note assures Hampshire College students that the school's alumni will support them." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760314/original/file-20260916-50-clcl68.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760314/original/file-20260916-50-clcl68.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760314/original/file-20260916-50-clcl68.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760314/original/file-20260916-50-clcl68.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760314/original/file-20260916-50-clcl68.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760314/original/file-20260916-50-clcl68.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760314/original/file-20260916-50-clcl68.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">A sticky note spotted at Hampshire College’s Harold F. Johnson Library on May 16, 2026, months before the school was slated to be closed for good, assured students that alumni would support them.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/amherst-ma-flyers-blanket-the-walls-of-harold-f-johnson-news-photo/2276384655?adppopup=true">Finn Gomez/The Boston Globe via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Higher education giving</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.case.org/system/files/media/inline/CASE%20Insights%20on%20VSE%2C%202025%20%20Key%20Findings.pdf">Donors contributed $79 billion</a> to colleges and universities in 2025, up 4% in constant dollars from the year before.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.philanthropy.com/news/colleges-raised-78-billion-89-of-funds-came-from-2-of-donors/">The richest Americans</a> dominate giving to higher education: <a href="https://www.theeduledger.com/latest-news/article/15822607/wealthy-donors-prop-up-university-funding-as-smallscale-giving-fades">89% of the funds raised came from only 2% of donors</a> in 2025.</p>

<p>Also in 2025, Phil and Penny Knight, the Nike co-founder and his wife, made what was then the largest single gift to a university in history when they gave the <a href="https://news.ohsu.edu/2025/08/14/ohsu-knight-cancer-institute-receives-record-2-billion-commitment-from-phil-and-penny-knight">Oregon Health &amp; Science University $2 billion for cancer research</a>.</p>

<p>On Sept. 30, 2026, investor Ken Griffin broke that record by giving <a href="https://www.cmu.edu/news/stories/archives/2026/september/griffins-landmark-gift-will-shape-the-future-of-higher-education">Carnegie Mellon University more than $3 billion</a> to build a new campus in Miami and meet some other priorities.</p>

<p>It’s hardly the only megagift a university has received in 2026: Michael and Susan Dell, whose fortune comes from his computer hardware company, gave the <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/michaeltnietzel/2026/04/21/michael-and-susan-dell-commit-750-million-to-the-university-of-texas/">University of Texas at Austin $750 million</a> for its medical center. The <a href="https://www.uoregon.edu/press/2026/knight-engineering/">Knights gave $1 billion</a> to the University of Oregon for a new engineering college. Software billionaire <a href="https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2026/01/largest-gift-university-history-names-cornell-david-duffield-college-engineering">David Duffield pledged $371 million to Cornell University</a>. And many other schools have drawn <a href="https://www.highereddive.com/news/biggest-donations-gifts-colleges-universities-2026/821000/">gifts in excess of $100 million</a>.</p>

<p>The vast majority of these huge gifts are <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/michaeltnietzel/2025/03/20/philanthropic-giving-to-us-colleges-increased-3-last-year/">reserved for specific purposes</a>. The share of totally <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-is-unrestricted-funding-two-philanthropy-experts-explain-16458">unrestricted gifts to colleges and universities</a>, those given with no strings attached, has been <a href="https://www.tiaa.org/public/institute/publication/2020/how-donors-give-higher-education">dwindling for decades</a>. <a href="https://www.case.org/research/surveys/voluntary-support-education-survey/VSE-2024">In 2024 it slipped below 7%</a>. Unrestricted giving <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p4_7fip_Cd0">did pick up somewhat in 2025</a>. Perhaps that was a sign that some donors were responding to federal funding cuts with their gifts.</p>

<h2>How donors can help</h2>

<p>In an article in <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/00091383.2026.2710571">Change: The Magazine of Higher Learning</a> in September 2026, we listed ideas for college and university fundraising efforts. These tie to three recommendations for donors – and not only those making multimillion-dollar gifts. </p>

<p><strong>1. Pooling donations</strong></p>

<p>Donations to colleges and universities don’t have to end in lots of zeros to make a big difference.</p>

<p>In 2015, the grassroots <a href="https://givinginstitute.org/the-story-of-saving-sweet-briar-or-dont-mess-with-the-vixen/">Saving Sweet Briar</a> campaign kept the small women’s college operating even after its trustees had voted to close it. The largest gift the rural Virginia school received was $2 million, and the smallest was $1.50 from a graduate’s grandchild. This is the exception rather than the rule. Financial pressures were too much for Hampshire College, a New England private college <a href="https://apnews.com/article/hampshire-college-closing-ken-burns-d2cc7834ead91f6220d1b17b980453b7">that is slated to close after the fall semester</a> of 2026, to withstand – even with a fundraising campaign and $5 million gift from alum and documentary filmmaker Ken Burns. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.case.org/system/files/media/file/Giving%20Day%202024%20Report%20Final%20v5%202025-10-29.pdf">Giving Days</a> are high-profile fundraising campaigns through which many alumni and other supporters raise millions. For example, Oregon State University <a href="https://fororegonstate.org/giving/giving-opportunities-and-featured-initiatives/dam-proud-day-impact-report-2026">Dam Proud Day 2026</a> drew 12,400 gifts and raised over $4.1 million. <a href="https://www.purdue.edu/studentsuccess/news/05_07_24.html">Purdue University’s annual “day of giving”</a> has generated nearly $500 million over the past decade. In 2024, it garnered $76 million from 32,000 donors.</p>

            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760319/original/file-20260916-50-zla3qk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A group of young women gather for a selfie." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760319/original/file-20260916-50-zla3qk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760319/original/file-20260916-50-zla3qk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=435&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760319/original/file-20260916-50-zla3qk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=435&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760319/original/file-20260916-50-zla3qk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=435&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760319/original/file-20260916-50-zla3qk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=546&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760319/original/file-20260916-50-zla3qk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=546&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760319/original/file-20260916-50-zla3qk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=546&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><strong>2. Donating with few or no strings attached</strong></p>

<p>Donations with few restrictions or none at all help colleges and universities meet their greatest needs.</p>

<p>Even if they’re mostly intended for a new building or to fund a particular program, <a href="https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED674510">large gifts can also include unrestricted portions</a> to help cover costs as needs arise and priorities change.</p>

<p><a href="https://alumni.brandeis.edu/giving/">Brandeis University</a>, <a href="https://give.myiu.org/iu-foundation/I320003566.html">Indiana University</a>, <a href="https://alumni.princeton.edu/stories/annual-giving-campaign-results-2526">Princeton University</a> and other schools encourage unrestricted annual gifts. These flexible funds are helping to cover <a href="https://giving.cornell.edu/why-give/impact/">research funding shortfalls</a> at Cornell University, <a href="https://giving.georgetown.edu/current-use-vs-endowment/">undergraduate scholarships</a> at Georgetown University and <a href="https://www.coa.edu/giving/">general operations</a> at the College of the Atlantic. </p>

<p>Novelist and philanthropist MacKenzie Scott, the former wife of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, has <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/media-advertising/articles/elon-musk-mackenzie-scott-giving-152505233.html">given more than $26 billion in unrestricted donations</a> to nonprofits, including to colleges and universities. <a href="https://www.theroot.com/mackenzie-scott-s-hbcu-giving-has-crossed-1-billion-an-2000125050">Historically Black colleges and universities</a> as well as other <a href="https://www.insidehighered.com/news/quick-takes/2025/12/15/mackenzie-scott-showers-colleges-more-gifts">schools with diverse student bodies</a>, such as Robeson Community College in rural North Carolina, Oklahoma’s Carl Albert State College and Wisconsin’s Fond du Lac Tribal and Community College, have received Scott’s big gifts.</p>

<p>In 1920, the trustees of Berea College, a private liberal arts school in Kentucky, <a href="https://magazine.berea.edu/campus-initiatives/century-old-decision-inspires-100-in-100-initiative/">passed a resolution</a> placing future unrestricted bequests, donations made through people’s estates, in the school’s endowment. Berea students do not pay for <a href="https://www.berea.edu/mountaineer-news/news/berea-college-launches-financial-freedom-pledge-creating-a-fully-funded-degree">tuition, fees, housing or food</a> – thanks in large part to those unrestricted donations.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/7AdJjvQS3Bo?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">All Berea College students get free tuition, and the small Kentucky school has also committed to covering all other attendance costs too.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><strong>3. Helping students afford all college costs so they can graduate</strong></p>

<p>Supporting students directly helps them go to college, <a href="https://www.insidehighered.com/news/students/retention/2025/12/04/6-year-graduation-rate-holds-steady">stay in school and graduate</a>. </p>

<p>Donors already make gifts that fund schools’ financial aid packages, with about <a href="https://www.case.org/research/surveys/case-insights-voluntary-support-education">$7 billion in gifts designated for this purpose in 2025</a>. But the colleges and universities that receive the most dollars from donors serve a small fraction of the nation’s undergraduate students – <a href="https://www.tiaa.org/content/dam/tiaa/institute/pdf/research-dialogue/2024-07/tiaa-institute-investigating-the-impact-of-philanthropic-giving-rd-213-shaker-july-2024.pdf">and not those from low-income families</a>. We recommend that donors consider making gifts to the thousands of colleges and universities, including community colleges, that don’t typically draw big donations and have endowments totaling in the millions, <a href="https://www.ibexinsights.co/data/rankings/all-endowment/">rather than billions, of dollars</a>.</p>

<p>Sometimes it takes more than tuition scholarships for students to graduate. Donors can pay for additional expenses, such as transportation and textbooks, and fund extra academic advising and mentoring. Billionaire philanthropists John and Laura Arnold’s <a href="https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/maricopa-community-colleges-mccf-and-arnold-ventures-announce-16-million-grant-to-support-student-outcomes-302794088.html">Commit2Completion grant program</a> at Arizona’s Maricopa Community Colleges addresses those kinds of often overlooked priorities.</p>

<p>You don’t have to be very wealthy to fund scholarships. Anyone can pitch in through platforms like <a href="https://scholarshipamerica.org/dollars-for-scholars-how-it-works/">Dollars for Scholars</a>. This program’s more than 400 chapters enable local donors to pool their gifts to help students raised in their communities pay college expenses. For example, a rural Minnesota chapter awarded $248,000 to 65 college-bound students in 2025.</p>

<p>There are also hundreds of other place-based “<a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/education/what-are-promise-programs-and-how-can-they-help-make-college-more-affordable">promise programs</a>” that provide tuition and fees scholarships to public colleges and universities in their areas and offer programming such as college readiness workshops and access to local employers.</p>

<p>Philanthropy can’t solve every problem higher education faces. But by giving together, donating with fewer strings attached and helping students pay their college expenses, alumni and other donors can be strategic in how they help.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/283427/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Pardoning of Israeli soldier evokes a long history of clemency for those who kill Palestinians</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765377/original/file-20261010-50-82noe6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C38%2C4792%2C3194&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Israeli soldier Elor Azaria, center, was convicted of manslaughter in 2017 after shooting dead a wounded Palestinian assailant.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/picture-taken-on-march-29-2016-shows-israeli-soldier-elor-news-photo/522255588?phrase=Elor%20Azaria&amp;adppopup=true">Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The <a href="https://apnews.com/article/israel-soldier-pardon-azaria-president-palestinian-killed-a8eb6b38bfc697554fd39d25c2b3faad">pardoning of Elor Azaria</a>, a former Israeli soldier convicted of killing a wounded Palestinian man in the occupied West Bank, comes with a history.</p>

<p>Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s decision itself – announced on Sept. 19, 2026 – came more than eight years after <a href="https://www.timesofisrael.com/hebron-shooter-azaria-may-be-freed-from-prison-tuesday/">Azaria left prison</a>. </p>

<p>The immediate effect is that it clears Azaria of his criminal record. But its public significance is broader – and reaches much further back.</p>

<p>I <a href="https://history.la.psu.edu/directory/tamir-sorek/">study how Israelis</a> have talked about Palestinian lives and deaths over the past century. In my <a href="https://www.waterstones.com/book/israels-genocidal-imagination/tamir-sorek/9781836743149">forthcoming book</a>, I trace a recurring idea: Palestinians are viewed as an obstacle to Israel’s territorial and security goals, and <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/netanyahu-partners-renew-calls-removal-gazans-israeli-election-nears-2026-09-04/">whose removal</a> <a href="https://foreignpolicy.com/2025/08/13/israel-netanyahu-gaza-displacement-palestinians-south-sudan/">can be imagined as necessary or justified</a>. Azaria’s pardon fits into this notion, showing how the state’s response to killing Palestinians can be expressed through the language of mercy for the perpetrator – and it is a pattern that goes back almost 80 years.</p>

<h2>A killing caught on camera</h2>

<p>The details of Azaria’s case are fairly straightforward. On March 24, 2016, Abdel Fattah al-Sharif and another Palestinian armed with knives <a href="https://www.timesofisrael.com/israel-returns-body-of-palestinian-attacker-killed-by-hebron-soldier/">attacked an Israeli soldier</a> in Hebron, in the occupied West Bank. Al-Sharif was shot and lay wounded on the ground. Minutes later, Azaria approached and shot him in the head. </p>

<p>Video of the killing <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2016/03/24/middleeast/video-israeli-soldier-palestinian-suspect">circulated widely</a>. An Israeli military court <a href="https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2017/02/21/516390968/israeli-soldier-who-killed-a-wounded-palestinian-is-sentenced-to-18-months">convicted Azaria of manslaughter in 2017</a> and sentenced him to 18 months in prison. He was released after serving nine months.</p>

<p>Justifying his decision, Herzog’s office <a href="https://edition.cnn.com/2026/09/20/world/israel-azaria-president-pardon-intl?iid=cnn_buildContentRecirc_end_recirc&amp;recs_exp=up-next-article-end&amp;tenant_id=related.en">cited the years that had passed</a>, Azaria’s expression of sorrow in his application for a pardon, and the approach of Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement.</p>

<p>Yet Azaria had said after his release that he <a href="https://www.i24news.tv/en/news/israel/diplomacy-defense/182963-180829-hebron-shooter-azaria-says-no-regrets-in-first-post-release-interview">would act the same way again</a>. While the conviction will remain part of the historical record, the pardon removes any lasting consequence for him.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A woman holds a banner showing a man's face." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765378/original/file-20261010-50-yf6aae.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765378/original/file-20261010-50-yf6aae.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=409&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765378/original/file-20261010-50-yf6aae.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=409&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765378/original/file-20261010-50-yf6aae.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=409&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765378/original/file-20261010-50-yf6aae.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=513&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765378/original/file-20261010-50-yf6aae.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=513&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765378/original/file-20261010-50-yf6aae.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=513&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Elor Azaria received support among far-right supporters and politicians.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/an-israeli-citizen-holds-a-banner-during-a-rally-in-tel-news-photo/522446860?phrase=Elor%20Azaria&amp;adppopup=true">Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Herzog’s decision was warmly received by some in Israel, where Azaria’s case had been <a href="https://www.i24news.tv/en/news/israel/society/artc-president-herzog-clears-elor-azaria-s-criminal-record">taken up by the political right</a>. </p>

<p>For human rights watchers, it is a worrying development. “The president’s decision is a clear demonstration that the Israeli justice system is neither willing nor able to enforce the law against soldiers who harm Palestinians,” <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/19/world/middleeast/israel-pardon-azaria.html">noted Ziv Stahl</a>, director of the Israeli human rights group Yesh Din.</p>

<p>However unequal that may appear to critics now, it is a trend with precedents reaching back to Israel’s founding.  </p>

<h2>Clemency after the 1948 war</h2>

<p>During the Arab-Israeli war between 1947 and 1949, some <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-nakba-at-75-palestinians-struggle-to-get-recognition-for-their-catastrophe-204782">750,000 Palestinians were uprooted from their homes</a>. It was an expulsion that could not have happened without extreme violence, including <a href="https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-540-68161-8_3">dozens of massacres</a> by Zionist militias and Israeli army.</p>

<p>The perpetrators were rarely, if ever, punished. </p>

<p>In November 1948, though, Israeli soldiers <a href="https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2019-03-15/ty-article/.premium/israeli-who-commanded-massacre-of-dozens-of-arab-captives-in-1948-dies-at-93/0000017f-e53c-dc7e-adff-f5bd6f8b0000">killed civilians in Hula</a>, a village in Lebanon. This time, the direct commander of the operation arrested the officer who ordered the massacre and complained about him. An Israeli military court convicted company commander <a href="https://www.akevot.org.il/en/news-item/case-19-48/">Shmuel Lahis of murdering 15 people</a> and sentenced him to seven years in prison.</p>

<p>On appeal, his sentence was reduced to one year. Israel’s first president, Chaim Weizmann, then <a href="https://www.lemkininstitute.com/single-post/terror-was-needed-to-make-arabs-leave-what-the-israeli-army-did-in-1948-revealed">canceled his prison sentence in 1950</a>. </p>

<p>Five years later, President Yitzhak Ben-Zvi pardoned Lahis. Decades later, in 1978, Lahis was appointed director general of the <a href="https://www.jewishagency.org/">Jewish Agency</a>, the primary Zionist organization promoting Jewish immigration and settlement in Israel. </p>

<p>These were distinct decisions, but together they show how a conviction for murdering Arab civilians eventually lost its practical and lasting consequences.</p>

<p>The Lahis case nevertheless established an early precedent for leniency toward an Israeli soldier convicted of murdering Arab civilians. It continued in the years that followed, when Israel, for several years after its independence, pursued an <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780198278504.001.0001">unofficial policy of shooting Palestinian refugees</a> who attempted to return to their homes, their land, or the property they had left behind. Costing the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780198278504.001.0001">lives of thousands until the mid-1950s</a>, this unofficial open-fire policy turned the new border into a lethal instrument for making the results of the expulsion permanent.</p>

<p>That precedent became clearer after the massacre at Kafr Qasim.</p>

<h2>The two legacies of Kafr Qasim</h2>

<p>On Oct. 29, 1956, Israeli Border Police <a href="https://questdev.palestine-studies.org/en/highlight/14334/kafr-qasim-29-october-1956">killed Palestinian citizens of Israel</a> returning home to Kafr Qasim, a village 12 miles (19 km) from Tel Aviv. Authorities had moved the start of a curfew forward without ensuring that villagers working outside knew about it. In all, Israeli troops killed 47 people. In the trial that followed, eight troops were convicted of murder and sentenced to prison terms ranging from seven to 17 years.</p>

<p>The ensuing military trial produced a principle taught for decades later in Israel: Soldiers must <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/43303033">refuse an order that is manifestly illegal</a>.</p>

<p>What happened after the convictions is less often remembered. The prison terms were reduced on appeal and, for some, reduced again by the military chief of staff. In November 1959, President Ben-Zvi shortened the sentences of the last two men still in prison, Shmuel Malinki and Gavriel Dahan. Both were released by March 1960. Less than 18 months after sentencing, every person convicted in the main trial was free.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Kafr Qasim, thus, left two legacies: The court drew a boundary against unlawful killing while other state authorities sharply limited the consequences for crossing it.</p>

<h2>Lenient punishment beyond pardons</h2>

<p>The pattern did not end with those early cases. Since the <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/gallery/2023/12/8/history-illustrated-the-first-intifada-against-israel">first Palestinian intifada</a>, or uprising, began in 1987, human rights organizations have <a href="https://www.un.org/unispal/document/auto-insert-209016/">documented how seldom</a> <a href="https://www.hindrajabfoundation.org/posts/the-illusion-of-accountability-israel-investigates-itself">investigations into Israeli soldiers’ killings</a> <a href="https://www.adalah.org/en/content/view/9048">of Palestinians resulted in prosecution</a>. </p>

<p>From the beginning of the second intifada in 2000 through March 2011, Israeli forces in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip <a href="https://www.btselem.org/firearms/20130409_soldier_convicted_for_shooting_udai_darawish">killed at least 3,024 Palestinians</a> who were not taking part in combat, according to the Israeli human rights organization B'Tselem. Of all such incidents, only 12 soldiers were indicted, and <a href="https://www.btselem.org/firearms/20130409_soldier_convicted_for_shooting_udai_darawish">not a single one was convicted of murder</a>.</p>

<p>My research points to the same pattern across a longer period. Throughout Israel’s history, even in the rare cases of conviction of a soldier or a policeman for killing Palestinians, the maximum time a perpetrator spent in prison was three years and four months.</p>

<p>This measures time served, rather than the sentences initially announced by courts – a distinction made especially clear by Kafr Qasim and reinforced by the Azaria case today. After all, the former military medic served just nine months of an 18-month sentence for the killing of a wounded Palestinian. And even then, was deemed to be suitable for a pardon.</p>

<p>In so doing, Herzog is nodding to the past, but also signaling to soldiers on the ground today that killing a Palestinian is forgivable. The pardon transforms what is sometimes presented as an aberration into part of the state’s moral order</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293623/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
