<title>More than 119 million Brazilians voted in the Oct. 4 election – including about 21,000 Florida residents</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764722/original/file-20261007-50-d5wawa.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3320%2C2213&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Nearly 9,000 Brazilian citizens voted at the polling place in Kissimmee, Fla., outside Orlando, on Oct. 4, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/brazilian-nationals-have-their-identification-verified-at-a-news-photo/2297963732?phrase=brazil%20election%20in%20us%202026&amp;adppopup=true">Gregg Newton/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-interactive/2026/oct/04/brazil-presidential-election-2026-first-round-live-results">More than 119 million Brazilians</a> voted on Oct. 4, 2026, in the national elections to select the country’s next president and the governors of all 27 states, among other government officials.</p>

<p>That’s nearly 75% of the approximately <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/amp/world/brazils-presidential-vote-pits-trump-ally-against-incumbent-lula">159 million</a> eligible voters. Unlike in the U.S., voting is mandatory in Brazil for <a href="https://aceproject.org/epic-en/CDCountry?set_language=en&amp;topic=VR&amp;country=BR">all citizens between the ages of 18 and 70</a>.</p>

<p>This includes nearly <a href="https://agenciabrasil.ebc.com.br/en/politica/noticia/2026-09/nearly-1m-brazilians-abroad-eligible-vote-2026-elections">1 million Brazilians who currently live outside the country</a>. About 265,000 Brazilians call the U.S. home, with small but growing communities in <a href="https://www.latintimes.com/brazilians-abroad-split-map-during-2026-elections-flavio-takes-us-lula-dominates-europe-599829">Boston, New York and Miami</a>.</p>

<p>Because neither incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva nor his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of <a href="https://theconversation.com/jair-bolsonaro-arrested-amid-fears-he-planned-to-flee-as-coup-trial-nears-conclusion-269554">disgraced former President Jair Bolsonaro</a>, <a href="https://g1.globo.com/politica/eleicoes/2026/apuracao/presidente.ghtml">managed to get over 50% of the votes</a>, Brazilians at home and abroad will have to turn out again on Oct. 25 for a runoff election.</p>

<p>Brazil does not have a long tradition of democracy. But it does have a secure and sophisticated election system. As a <a href="https://liberalarts.du.edu/about/people/rafael-r-ioris">scholar of Latin American history and politics</a>, and a Brazilian citizen living in the U.S., I watched these elections with great interest.</p>

<h2>No voting by mail</h2>

<p>Brazilians living abroad are required by law to vote, but they may not cast ballots by mail or online. In many countries, Brazilian consulates serve as the polling places for the diaspora population. Because the U.S. is so spread out, the Brazilian government sets up <a href="https://despachante55.com/en/onde-votar-nos-eua-os-15-postos-eleitorais-brasileiros/">15 polling places in 12 states</a>. Two of these are in Florida – one in the Orlando area, where about 26,000 Brazilian voters live, and one in Miami, which is home to the third-largest concentration of Brazilians in the U.S., with more than 40,000 registered voters. </p>

<p>Voting takes place in a single day – always a Sunday – through electronic voting machines, and results are known within a few hours. Though it is compulsory, the penalty for not voting is just a small fine – about US$1 – and as long as a citizen notifies the government within two months of the election that they did not vote, they remain in good legal standing.</p>

<p>So it’s not surprising that only about 75,000 Brazilians – roughly 28% of eligible voters – cast their ballots in the U.S. on Oct. 4.</p>

<p>It’s unclear whether U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations prevented people from voting, though <a href="https://www.cnnbrasil.com.br/blogs/priscila-yazbek/internacional/abstencao-nos-eua-sobe-e-fica-em-7155-em-meio-a-temor-sobre-o-ice/">some Brazilians say</a> they believe fear of ICE contributed to a lower turnout than in 2022, when more than 37% of eligible voters cast their ballots. Organizations for expats in the U.S. warned Brazilians that <a href="https://despachante55.com/en/onde-votar-nos-eua-os-15-postos-eleitorais-brasileiros/">if their immigration status was precarious</a>, they should not vote.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764720/original/file-20261007-60-aj95g7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="people walking by a mural with pictures of two men together" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764720/original/file-20261007-60-aj95g7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764720/original/file-20261007-60-aj95g7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764720/original/file-20261007-60-aj95g7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764720/original/file-20261007-60-aj95g7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764720/original/file-20261007-60-aj95g7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764720/original/file-20261007-60-aj95g7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764720/original/file-20261007-60-aj95g7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A mural outside a polling place in Sao Paulo shows Donald Trump and Flávio Bolsonaro as a team.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/several-people-walk-past-a-wall-with-images-of-us-president-news-photo/2297973113?phrase=brazil%20trump&amp;adppopup=true">Photo by Pablo Porciuncula/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>How the US diaspora voted</h2>

<p>What is clear is the importance of this election for the future of Latin America’s largest economy and society, as well as for the future of Brazil-U.S. relations. If reelected, Lula is likely to continue to <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/10/04/nx-s1-5989593/brazils-election-could-shift-its-ties-with-the-u-s-and-china">resist overt pressures from Washington</a> to weaken Brazil’s economic ties with China.</p>

<p>On the other hand, Flávio Bolsonaro has signaled that he plans to have <a href="https://g1.globo.com/mundo/noticia/2026/10/07/trump-expande-influencia-na-america-do-sul-com-8-presidentes-alinhados-a-ele-flavio-bolsonaro-pode-se-tornar-o-9o.ghtml">much closer relations with the U.S</a>. That is why President Donald Trump <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/04/donald-trump-western-hemisphere-brazil-elections-lula-bolsonaro">would prefer to have a Bolsonaro</a> in power, so that the U.S. influence in Latin America may be further consolidated. </p>

<p>Among Brazilian voters who were abroad on Election Day, Lula won in 64 out of 101 countries where voting was made available by Brazilian diplomatic authorities. But Flávio Bolsonaro won in some of the nations with the <a href="https://g1.globo.com/mundo/noticia/2026/10/06/lula-venceu-em-64-paises-flavio-bolsonaro-em-36-mapa-mostra-como-foi-a-eleicao-no-exterior.ghtml">largest numbers of Brazilian residents</a>. This includes the U.S., Japan and neighboring countries in South America. </p>

<p>In the U.S., Brazilian voters cast 45,004 ballots for Flávio Bolsonaro and 23,335 for Lula. This seems to be another indication of the <a href="https://theconversation.com/brazil-election-authoritarian-right-gain-an-edge-fueled-by-voter-apathy-and-discontent-293655">polarization that has shaped this key election</a> and, more broadly, the general political context of Brazil in the past few years.</p>

<h2>Where Brazil goes next</h2>

<p>I was not surprised to see that Flávio Bolsonaro finished in the lead on Oct. 4, as the electoral pendulum across the region <a href="https://theconversation.com/brazil-elections-2026-first-round-victories-demand-a-commitment-to-democracy-by-the-far-right-that-has-not-yet-been-made-293548">has been swinging to the right of the political spectrum</a> for some time.</p>

<p>Even though Lula managed to <a href="https://g1.globo.com/politica/eleicoes/2022/apuracao/brasil/apuracao-pelo-brasil/">defeat Jair Bolsonaro</a> in 2022, <a href="https://theconversation.com/brazil-coup-charges-could-end-bolsonaros-political-career-but-they-wont-extinguish-bolsonarismo-250478">Bolsonarismo</a> – the extreme-right political movement that carries his name – has remained <a href="https://jovempan.com.br/colunistas/eliseu-caetano/dinastia-bolsonaro-ganha-forca-e-chama-atencao-da-imprensa-internacional-apos-1o-turno/">the most influential political force in the country</a>. This is a right-wing movement whose leaders, especially members of the Bolsonaro family, have openly and consistently <a href="https://www.npr.org/2018/10/26/660984573/with-memories-of-dictatorship-some-brazilians-fear-a-hard-right-turn">called for the revival of Brazil’s military regime</a> that ruled the country from the mid-1960s to mid-1980s.</p>

<p>Now that Flávio Bolsonaro, an otherwise irrelevant senator from the state of Rio de Janeiro, where the staunch political base of the Bolsonaros is located, has <a href="https://resultados.tse.jus.br/oficial/app/index.html#/eleicao/6257/uf/br/cargo/1/vis/nominal/resultados">finished ahead of Lula in the first round of elections</a>, it seems clear that the extreme right has the upper hand in Brazil today.</p>

<p>A few years ago, Brazil seemed on track to <a href="https://pepsic.scielo.org/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&amp;pid=S0486-641X2018000400008">becoming a mature democracy</a>, after having held several electoral cycles with peaceful transfers of power to opposition candidates.</p>

<p>But now, considering the <a href="https://sur.conectas.org/a-democracia-por-um-fio-resistencia-e-reconstrucao-no-brasil-pos-bolsonaro/">lack of commitment to democratic traditions in the Bolsonarismo movement</a>, this trend risks being derailed, ironically, by means of a democratic election.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293494/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

About 265,000 Brazilians call the U.S. home, with small but growing communities in Boston, New York and Miami

Because neither incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva nor his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of disgraced former President Jair Bolsonaro , managed to get over 50% of the votes , Brazilians at home and abroad will have to turn out again on Oct. 25 for a runoff election
Brazil does not have a long tradition of democracy
But it does have a secure and sophisticated election system
As a scholar of Latin American history and politics , and a Brazilian citizen living in the U.S., I watched these elections with great interest
No voting by mail Brazilians living abroad are required by law to vote, but they may not cast ballots by mail or online
In many countries, Brazilian consulates serve as the polling places for the diaspora population
Because the U.S. is so spread out, the Brazilian government sets up 15 polling places in 12 states

Two of these are in Florida – one in the Orlando area, where about 26,000 Brazilian voters live, and one in Miami, which is home to the third-largest concentration of Brazilians in the U.S., with more than 40,000 registered voters
Voting takes place in a single day – always a Sunday – through electronic voting machines, and results are known within a few hours

Though it is compulsory, the penalty for not voting is just a small fine – about US$1 – and as long as a citizen notifies the government within two months of the election that they did not vote, they remain in good legal standing
So it’s not surprising that only about 75,000 Brazilians – roughly 28% of eligible voters – cast their ballots in the U.S. on Oct. 4

Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations prevented people from voting, though some Brazilians say they believe fear of ICE contributed to a lower turnout than in 2022, when more than 37% of eligible voters cast their ballots
Organizations for expats in the U.S. warned Brazilians that if their immigration status was precarious , they should not vote
A mural outside a polling place in Sao Paulo shows Donald Trump and Flávio Bolsonaro as a team

Photo by Pablo Porciuncula/AFP via Getty Images How the US diaspora voted What is clear is the importance of this election for the future of Latin America’s largest economy and society, as well as for the future of Brazil-U.S. relations
If reelected, Lula is likely to continue to resist overt pressures from Washington to weaken Brazil’s economic ties with China
On the other hand, Flávio Bolsonaro has signaled that he plans to have much closer relations with the U.S
That is why President Donald Trump would prefer to have a Bolsonaro in power, so that the U.S. influence in Latin America may be further consolidated
Among Brazilian voters who were abroad on Election Day, Lula won in 64 out of 101 countries where voting was made available by Brazilian diplomatic authorities
But Flávio Bolsonaro won in some of the nations with the largest numbers of Brazilian residents
This includes the U.S., Japan and neighboring countries in South America
In the U.S., Brazilian voters cast 45,004 ballots for Flávio Bolsonaro and 23,335 for Lula
This seems to be another indication of the polarization that has shaped this key election and, more broadly, the general political context of Brazil in the past few years

Where Brazil goes next I was not surprised to see that Flávio Bolsonaro finished in the lead on Oct. 4, as the electoral pendulum across the region has been swinging to the right of the political spectrum for some time
Even though Lula managed to defeat Jair Bolsonaro in 2022, Bolsonarismo – the extreme-right political movement that carries his name – has remained the most influential political force in the country

This is a right-wing movement whose leaders, especially members of the Bolsonaro family, have openly and consistently called for the revival of Brazil’s military regime that ruled the country from the mid-1960s to mid-1980s

Now that Flávio Bolsonaro, an otherwise irrelevant senator from the state of Rio de Janeiro, where the staunch political base of the Bolsonaros is located, has finished ahead of Lula in the first round of elections , it seems clear that the extreme right has the upper hand in Brazil today
A few years ago, Brazil seemed on track to becoming a mature democracy , after having held several electoral cycles with peaceful transfers of power to opposition candidates
But now, considering the lack of commitment to democratic traditions in the Bolsonarismo movement , this trend risks being derailed, ironically, by means of a democratic election

title: Why the right turned on Indian Americans
excerpt: Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor of Ohio, at a campaign event in Vandalia, Ohio, on October 3, 2026. | Jessica Phelps/Bloomberg via Getty
body: Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor of Ohio, at a campaign event in Vandalia, Ohio, on October 3, 2026. | Jessica Phelps/Bloomberg via Getty Images In early October, Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor of Ohio, went for a classic “politician on the stump” move: He picked up a kid
Ramaswamy fumbled the boy a bit , producing a clip that quickly went viral on social media
The next day, Ramaswamy posted a picture of himself with his son in his arms on social media
But many of the responses were ugly — racist attacks against Ramaswamy that drew on anti-Indian stereotypes

It was the latest example of a broader shift on the right, where Indian Americans and Indian immigrants have become a conspicuous target of online conservative anger. “The people who had negative stereotypes about Indians in their mind said, ‘Hey, look, the guy can’t even pick up a kid…he can’t even act like a normal American family man,’” freelance journalist Zaid Jilani told Today, Explained co-host Noel King

Jilani, who recently wrote about the surge in anti-Indian racism for Vox, joined the podcast for a conversation about how he sees the bigotry as rooted in status envy, how Indian Americans and Indian immigrants are responding, and his surprisingly hopeful outlook for the future
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
American racism is very interesting, always has been

And there is a type that says, immigrants are dirty, they come here, they’re uneducated, they leach off the government, they’re taking our resources.  The stereotype of Indian immigrants to America and Indian Americans is people who go to college, people who often have advanced degrees, people who often live in nice neighborhoods, make good money, are family-values people.  Why do you think these values that seem as if they mesh with what Republicans want are so triggering to people these days? Is it just yes, but they’re brown? I think that is a component of it

I spoke to one Indian American advocate who told me that Indians and South Asians more broadly are visible minorities, right? If you think about other minorities who are highly successful, that’s not always the case.  For instance, I think that Jewish Americans have been known since the late 20th century as being a successful minority group, but they’re not necessarily highly visible
If [Texas Railroad Commissioner candidate] Bo French saw a bunch of white people in the stadium with the Longhorns, I’m not sure he would be picking out who’s Protestant, who’s Catholic, who’s Jewish
But with Indian Americans, they are highly visible
That being said, I think you have to think about where Indian Americans are in society and the kind of feelings that can create among everyone else
If you look, for instance, at Silicon Valley, the major tech companies, Microsoft, Google — the head of [Microsoft’s] Xbox division is an Indian American woman now

You have a group of people who I think are in many ways a very micro minority — we’re talking about 1 percent to 2 percent of the United States — visibly rising into so many positions that I think a lot of people have typically associated with white folks
White people generally run the Fortune 500, white folks run the universities, white folks are the most successful doctors and engineers

And that was true for the 20th century.  But when you start seeing a much larger influx of Asian immigrants, starting with liberalization of immigration laws in the ’60s, but also when there was a rapid growth of the technology sector in the early 2000s, you start to understand a little bit more where the resentment comes from because it’s more, I would say, analogically similar to antisemitism than it is to the racism that Mexican Americans face or the racism that Black Americans face.  “It’s a much larger anti-globalization backlash on the right, not only when it comes to things like immigration, but also trade and tariffs and restrictions like that.” It’s not that Indian Americans are necessarily being stereotyped as antisocial, criminal, coming here illegally, so on and so forth

It’s more that they’re being seen as a status threat to a lot of particularly middle-class Americans, people who want their kids to rise to the top of their school, who want their kids to have the corner office

They want their kids to be able to get the most prestigious positions.  I think in the minds of a lot of these people, not only now does their kid have to compete with all the other normal white kids in their community, they have to compete against the entire world
It’s a much larger anti-globalization backlash on the right, not only when it comes to things like immigration, but also trade and tariffs and restrictions like that
When you talked to Indian Americans for this piece , what did you hear from them that surprised you? Probably the most surprising thing was how much pragmatism they responded to all of this with
Nine times out of 10, when you have stories about racism, the victims of racism are outraged — understandably and justifiably outraged
They certainly don’t want to see restrictions on the right to immigration, or other things to limit their numbers, which is the end point of a lot of this
At the same time, I think a lot of the people I spoke to were very upfront
They’re like, “Hey, look, we have found a lot of success in America
We got the golden ticket to be able to come here, for our kids to study here, to be able to really seek these opportunities, but we understand what’s happening in the economy
We understand there’s a lot of people who are struggling and then they see us rising to the top of all these organizations
They see us with our kind of well-ensconced place in the economy
And I think it’s important for us not to flaunt our success that much.” At least a couple people said something to that respect
They almost empathize with the people who were hating on them

It struck me as such a classic immigrant pragmatism that you see from the first or second wave of immigrants: people who realize that they are newcomers to a society or maybe their parents were newcomers to a society, and that there is a certain level of grappling they have to do with, “Hey, how can we continue to have success? How can we continue to grind and resist this racism, but also not rub it in people’s faces that we’re doing well because the more they do that, the tougher it can be?” A number brought up Vivek Ramaswamy in the sense that Vivek happened to go on social media and talk about what he felt like were deficiencies in American culture when it comes to studying, when it comes to working hard

I think that in bringing that up, they were saying that that wasn’t particularly helpful because whatever positive aspects there may be to Indian immigrant culture, we shouldn’t talk about them in ways that denigrate other people because that’s obviously going to rub people the wrong way
You’re making the point that some of the surge in anti-Indian racism on the right is about status anxiety
I was listening to this podcast that Chris Rufo and Jonathan Keeperman did
These are two influential right-wing activists

They called it “The Indian Question” — a lot of people’s eyebrows shot up — and they seem to be making the argument that it is about status anxiety.  They also were making less coherent arguments about how it’s un-American to study for the spelling bee, which is what South Asian kids do, and that white kids are more American because they play football, then they go to a party and get drunk, and then they get 1,500 on the SAT
I’m assuming you watched that exchange

What did you make of that? There’s a certain level of coping mechanism being deployed there in the sense that they are trying to explain the success of Indian Americans as a deficiency: “Maybe they’re getting to the top schools, but that’s because they’re shut in all day studying.” But it’s not really true that Indian Americans are necessarily cloistered into unhealthy habits
They’re actually finding success across society

title: The man who will likely be the next House speaker, explained
excerpt: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks to the press on the steps of the US Capitol on September 30, 2026. | Finn Gomez/Getty Images Barring a catastrophic
body: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks to the press on the steps of the US Capitol on September 30, 2026. | Finn Gomez/Getty Images Barring a catastrophic midterm polling miss, Democrats are on track to win a majority in the House of Representatives next month

Come the new Congress in January, that will mean a new House speaker — and if all goes to plan, that will be current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries.  If elected, Jeffries, from New York, will be the first Black speaker of the House

Though Jeffries has been in Congress for nearly 14 years now — and many of those years have been spent in Democratic leadership — he also remains something of an enigma.  The New Yorker’s Jason Zengerle profiled Jeffries back in May

He spoke with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram about who Jeffries really is, his path to what would be a historic speakership, and what he really stands for.   Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
In your profile of potential future Speaker of the House Hakeem Jeffries, you start with a story that people might find surprising
And I was wondering if you could tell us said story. [Jeffries] was in Florida, raising money, which is one of his central responsibilities as a minority leader
And he was being driven to a Democratic donor’s house in Palm Beach

And while he was being driven there, he got an alert on his phone letting him know that Donald Trump had posted a message to Truth Social in which he rehashed a bunch of the 2020 election conspiracies

More significantly, [Trump] had included a depiction of Barack Obama and Michelle Obama as apes .  Jeffries has this reputation for being a very calm, deliberate, not angry person, oftentimes to his detriment
I think a lot of Democratic partisans wish he would be more angry
But the way he told me the story, he was legitimately pissed off
And he realized that he needed to respond in some way

And he didn’t think that a tweet would be sufficient.  He wanted to do an Instagram post, and he looked into his aide’s iPhone, and he said, “ Fuck Donald Trump .” And as soon as he was done recording the video, I think he started to have second thoughts
And they sent the video up to Washington for a social media team to edit, and he told them, “Let’s bleep out the word fuck.” And for him, it was a smashing social media success

I was in his office in the Capitol six days later, and he was telling me this story and basking in some of the reflected glory and talking about all the social media love and talking about the real-world love

But then he kind of paused, and he said something like, “You know, but I still haven’t heard from my mom, and I’m a little worried about that.” Which I thought captured him pretty well. “I don’t think you’re going to see a new Hakeem Jeffries if he’s speaker

I think he’s going to, especially rhetorically, perform the same way he has before.” Why did you want to start your profile of him with that story? What does it tell us about who this individual is? I thought it captured the dilemma he faces in some ways, just in the sense that he is this very deliberate, calculated political figure, very conventional
And he is operating in a political space these days that doesn’t really reward or appreciate that approach.  Oftentimes that approach is not successful
I think he’s trying to adapt to the new rules of the road, and he’s kind of doing it in fits and starts, and sometimes he’s more successful than others

But I still think, even when he is successful, he has some qualms about it.  How long has Hakeem Jeffries wanted to be speaker of the House? When he got to Congress, in 2012, he definitely wanted to become a player
He wanted to be in leadership, chair a committee, whatever
He was someone who had his eye on that.  But at the same time, the Congressional Black Caucus had started to think a little bit differently about what they could achieve in Congress
For a long time, they wanted their members to get chairmanships and things like that, or maybe be majority whip
But by the time Jeffries got there, they started to think that we could actually get a speaker
And his arrival kind of coincided with this realization on the part of the CBC

And I think a lot of CBC members viewed Jeffries as a potential future speaker, and they started to groom him for that.  Pretty soon after that, Nancy Pelosi started to think of him as someone who would be a good member of her leadership team

And I think by 2018, that’s when it really became apparent that he was going to be someone who could potentially be speaker.  What does he actually stand for as the most powerful Democrat in the House? I think, quite intentionally, he doesn’t stand for anything
I think that in some ways has been key to his success
He has managed for the most part to avoid being kind of pigeonholed or put anywhere on the ideological spectrum
He is very critical of the far left of the party, especially the DSA

He views the DSA as college-educated young white people who are coming to Brooklyn and displacing older Black working-class people.  I was talking to this former Democratic congressional aide and basically asking this person the question you’re asking me: What does he stand for? And this person was trying to explain it and finally just was sort of exasperated, and he said he’s intentionally trying not to stand for anything
We don’t have a lot of case studies for how he manages his caucus because they haven’t been in power
But I think maybe one of the most telling examples was the shutdown, because Democrats were, in a way, the power brokers there

That was probably his greatest success as minority leader.  When Trump took office for the second time, especially for those first few months, I think all of the congressional Democrats, and Jeffries especially, were really on their heels
They could not figure out how to deal with this guy and what they were going to do to stop him
Jeffries was even complaining that he didn’t have any leverage

But then he eventually realized that a shutdown would be at least a little bit of leverage.  The real question was, what was the shutdown going to be about? And there were a lot of Democratic members of Congress who wanted it to be about authoritarianism or corruption
They wanted it to be at all these different issues
And Jeffries was really insistent that we need to make this about one issue, and we need to make it about healthcare.  The Democrats were the ones who caused the shutdown

title: The liver transplant system tried to fix its sex bias. Did it work?
excerpt: In theory, getting a donor liver in the United States when you need one should be an extremely equitable process: The sickest patients with the greatest chance
body: In theory, getting a donor liver in the United States when you need one should be an extremely equitable process: The sickest patients with the greatest chance to benefit from a donated organ should jump to the front of the line regardless of their gender, race, or other factors.  But in practice, things look quite different.  One study from 2020 showed that women were 8.6 percent more likely than men to die waiting for a liver transplant and 14.4 percent less likely to receive a deceased donor liver transplant compared to men
That gap may not seem enormous, but it still represents a significant disparity
As it turns out, it’s rooted in the very system that’s supposed to make the process fairer, a process that unintentionally ranks women lower on the waitlist for livers
The system in question is known as the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD)
The scoring model has been used since 2002 to rank candidates on the waiting list based on how likely they are to survive without a liver transplant in the short term
The higher your score, the reasoning goes, the sicker you are and the more urgently you need a liver transplant
One of the values used to calculate the score is creatinine — a waste product made by muscles as they break down proteins or other compounds to release energy
In medicine, the creatinine levels in your blood are used to determine how well your kidneys are functioning because they process and remove creatinine

And this is where the system designed for equity gets a little less than equitable for some patients.  Creatinine levels are affected by muscle mass, and women typically have lower muscle mass than men
A man and woman experiencing the same level of kidney dysfunction will therefore have different levels of creatinine in the body

The MELD model doesn’t take this difference into account — and so lower levels of creatinine in a woman’s blood can make her seem healthier than she is, bumping her farther down the liver waiting list. Ray Kim, a transplant hepatologist at Mayo Clinic in Arizona who developed the original system, debuted a new model called MELD 3.0
The model not only seeks to address the sex disparity in liver access but also improve the accuracy of scores for all patients
Among other changes, it takes into account the sex of the transplant candidate and uses it to adjust the MELD score by 1.33 points for women
This is meant to address the difference in creatinine levels between men and women and provide a more accurate understanding of how sick a female patient really is

Simple fix, right? Even though MELD 3.0 took the sex disparity in liver access seriously and developed changes to combat it, early research on its efficacy found that even this new and improved system hasn’t yet brought men and women to parity on the liver waitlist

And the problem may lie less with what MELD 3.0 did than with what it did not do, prompting the question: Are we focusing on the wrong problem? Sex matters…but so does size Before the MELD score, liver transplants were largely conducted on a first-come, first-served basis
Those who were added to the waiting list first, received livers first
If a really sick candidate was added to the waiting list late, say because of delayed diagnosis, they would almost certainly die while waiting for a liver to become available
The original MELD fixed that problem by creating a measure of urgency that was easy to calculate
The initial model used three main blood test values — bilirubin, creatinine, and a measure of blood clotting time — and later improvements also took into account the sodium level
Key takeaways Women are more likely than men to die waiting for a liver transplant in part because the system used to rank candidates on the liver waiting list underestimates how sick women are
In 2023, the liver transplant system adopted a new version of that scoring model, which adds 1.33 points to women’s scores to correct for differences in muscle mass between the sexes
Early research shows that the new model increased transplant rates for women, but the gains were transient
Experts say that the score is only part of the problem
A donated liver has to physically fit inside the body receiving it, so smaller candidates end up waiting longer for a liver they can accept
The organ allocation system currently has no way to prioritize smaller livers toward smaller patients, who are more often women
Fixing this is likely the key to ensuring equitable liver access for men and women
Traditionally, the MELD model assigns a score between 6 and 40 to liver transplant candidates
MELD 3.0 adds 1.33 points to women’s scores to account for the differences in creatinine levels between the sexes
The new model also measures albumin, an additional biomarker, and adjusts for interactions between the different variables

Sommer Gentry, a professor at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and contributor to the paper on MELD 3.0, said that using sophisticated algorithms with more biomarkers not only helps to better predict risk for women, but using a more accurate model also benefits the whole population
The researchers estimate that this fine-tuned MELD 3.0 model will reduce at least 20 waiting list deaths per year
Last year, around 800 liver transplant candidates died while waiting for a liver
But creatinine is only one of the two main problems that create a disparity in liver access for women
The second, Gentry says, is body size, an issue that’s not addressed by MELD 3.0
A transplanted liver has to physically fit inside the body of a recipient, and women are typically smaller than men, so a very large liver cannot be offered to a small woman

But the reverse is not necessarily true because receiving a liver that is small for the potential recipient doesn’t typically harm the candidate.     “The smaller you are, the less likely you are to be offered something that’s actually going to work for you,” Gentry said, adding that women end up waiting longer to receive a liver that will actually fit their body

Part of the conversation on sex disparity in liver access is based around which of the two problems — creatinine or body-size interventions — to fix first, and whether it is possible to create equity by addressing just one of the two, Gentry said

MELD 3.0 was an attempt to remove the former barrier. “I think that some other papers are coming out that suggest that perhaps the other aspect of size matching is still a concern and still possibly not addressed by the resulting liver transplant system,” Gentry said

title: Your kid wants to go vegan. Should you let them?
excerpt: Hi readers! Shayla Love here, science journalist and longtime fan of Your Mileage May Vary
body: Hi readers! Shayla Love here, science journalist and longtime fan of Your Mileage May Vary
I’m honored to be subbing for Sigal Samuel while she’s out on parental leave
I’m diving into your questions as a way to help understand human nature and our choices through multiple lenses: philosophical, psychological, and beyond
Please send in any emotional, body/brain, sociological, perceptual, or other kind of life quandaries you might have
Neither of her parents are even vegetarian — we’re “free range chicken/grass fed beef” types
She has learned about veganism from friends at school, and seems to have come to her position more or less on her own
I want to encourage her ethical choices, but her mother and I agree that children should be introduced to new foods and flavors at this age
She has no allergies or intolerances that we know of
I worry that making accommodations for her dietary restriction may lead to a lifetime of picky eating, even if hers is a reasonable and ethical approach
She seems to be uncomfortable when her mother or I cook meat for meals we share, even if we make her another option
What should I do to support my daughter? Dear Hold the Beef,  When I was around your daughter’s age, I went to Hawaii with my parents
One night, we ate dinner on the beach, and we watched as a pig was dug up from an underground steam oven
I was horrified to see its face and nose; most of the meat I had eaten so far in my life didn’t resemble the animal it came from

A few years later, I became a vegetarian, and then in my 20s, a vegan.  Have a question you want answered in the next Your Mileage May Vary column? Fill out this anonymous form ! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions
Sign up here! I share this story to reveal my slight bias in answering your question, but also my understanding of the ethical awakening your daughter might be experiencing
As you figure out how to talk to your child about what she decides to eat, we can at least table discussing the pros and cons of veganism itself

Instead, you should think about what amount of autonomy your child should have, and whether the moral decision-making she wants to engage in matches with her current stage of development.  People don’t turn 18 and then suddenly start engaging morally with the world
As we grow up, we try to understand right and wrong in fits and spurts

Lawrence Kohlberg, a 20th-century American psychologist, is best known for attempting to track a person’s moral development throughout their life.  Kohlberg presented people with hypothetical dilemmas in order to come up with six moral stages
In one example, he asked people of different ages about a dying woman who could be cured by a drug that was cheap to make, but that a manufacturer was charging an exorbitant fee for
The woman’s husband ends up stealing the drug

Is that right or wrong? Kohlberg observed that in answering questions like this, young children have what he called a “preconventional morality”: Their notions of right and wrong are dictated by what their parents think, and the avoidance of punishment when breaking those rules

For instance, the main reason not to throw your dinner on the ground or hit your brother was to avoid consequences from parents, not a feeling that there’s something wrong about that action.  Kohlberg thought this stage lasted until around age 9, and in the next period, children began to understand that there isn’t just one correct action, but that people could have different moral ideas based on their social context

To sum up the rest of the stages quickly, each one progresses to encompass more views — like the moral agreements necessary to make a society function — and more complexity — like the realization that a seemingly immoral action can ultimately be moral, like stealing medicine for one’s wife.  It’s useful to pinpoint where your daughter finds herself on Kohlberg’s timeline
It sounds like she’s in the shift from the first stage and into the later ones
What you’ve decided — that it’s okay to eat meat if it’s free-range or grass-fed — is no longer sufficient for your daughter in terms of guiding her own actions
That can be a jarring moment for a parent, but at least, according to Kohlberg, it’s a sign of maturation
Your child should , at this age, start to consider her friends, as well as the experiences she’s had without you, when making an ethical choice.  But I’m her parent , you may protest

That doesn’t necessarily mean that your job is to exclusively provide black-and-white directives.  Alison Gopnik, a psychologist and philosopher at the University of California Berkeley, has written about the unique perspective and personhood of children (including babies)
In her book The Gardener and the Carpenter , she questions how people have come to define the act of parenting as having specific goals in mind for their children
This approach is like being a carpenter, she writes, who follows instructions to assemble a predetermined piece of furniture
She argues that parenting is more like gardening: You cultivate the soil and the environment and realize that you could produce any number of different flowers, fruits, or vegetables

Growth is the point, not a by-the-book final product.  I see Gopnik in alignment with Jean-Jacques Rousseau, the 18th-century philosopher whose novel Émile, or On Education surprised its readers by advocating for a freer and child-centered approach to teaching. Émile, a young wealthy boy, is tutored — in high contrast to the expectations of the day — without strict rules
Rousseau thought you couldn’t make a child turn into an adult any faster, and it was foolish to try

He also thought that children had to learn by having their own experiences out in the world, and learning from those, rather than just overly didactic lessons.  As your daughter dips her toe into the morality of eating meat, Rousseau would also remind you not to expect her to have the most mature ideas about veganism or her meal plan
She is still young, and may just have come across an idea that feels ethically important to her
Your role as her parent is to help her develop her nuanced morality, a process Kohlberg suggests will continue, and not steer her towards one way of eating over another
Be Gopnik’s dietary gardener, not carpenter.  Of course, parents do have rights over their children, and an obligation to keep them safe
When we’re young, we’re not always equipped to make the right choice (some would argue this continues into adulthood, too)
If your daughter decided to take up smoking cigarettes, for instance, you would step in because her choice would negatively affect her health

title: The company behind Skittles might be to blame for your big vet bills
excerpt: Nova, a 6-month-old Australian shepherd, gets vaccinated at the Community Animal Medicine Project, a low-cost veterinary clinic in Northridge, Los Angeles, on J
body: Nova, a 6-month-old Australian shepherd, gets vaccinated at the Community Animal Medicine Project, a low-cost veterinary clinic in Northridge, Los Angeles, on July 7, 2026. | Hans Gutknecht/MediaNews Group/The Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images Whenever I have dinner with friends, the conversation always ends up on one of three topics: how hard dating is , the hunt for affordable housing , or an update on everyone’s pets
The last on that list includes cute photos and veterinarian updates
I love hearing about my friends’ cats and dogs
But I also have to admit that I just don’t get it
I never have. (We won’t discuss the ill-fated caterpillar in elementary school.) I’m in the minority: Over half of American households have pets
Which means that over half of American households have also seen the cost of pet care go up in recent years.   Helaine Olen is the proud pet parent of a Havanese poodle mix named Barney Rubble

She’s also the managing editor at the American Economic Liberties Project, an antitrust organization, and she says people often aren’t prepared for how expensive it can get.  Some of it is inflation, Olen says, but veterinary care is a major factor. “The same medical advances that have kept us alive longer and we consider miracles — whether it’s cancer drugs or stem cell therapies or various pharmaceuticals — the same is true for your cats and dogs,” Olen says
Decades ago, a cat having an MRI was unheard of; now, it’s common
But it’s not just expanded access and improved technology that’s driving prices up

Olen says that who’s behind that healthcare is a factor. “Big corporations and private equity have seen all of this, know that people say they will do anything for their pets, know that they think of their pets as children, and they have rushed into the sector,” she told Vox

So how did private equity get involved in the lives of our pets? And what happens when the prices keep climbing? We discuss that and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me , Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.  Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Olen, edited for length and clarity
You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts
If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545
What kind of costs are we talking about? When your pet is young, you’re probably spending several hundred dollars a year for various vaccines, spay and neuter, annual checkups
But the real costs start coming in as they get older and they need maintenance.  For tooth cleaning, pets need to be put under anesthesia
That will be even higher if a pet’s tooth has to be removed.  I’ve spoken to people whose pets have back legs that have collapsed or disc herniations
You can easily be out over $10,000 on a surgery
You can easily spend four figures on a 24-hour overnight
I spoke to somebody who was quoted $3,500 a night for just an observational overnight
You mentioned that some of this comes down to who owns pet clinics and how that’s changing
Who owns them now? Traditionally, it was an independent practice
But in the past 10 to 15 years, big corporations and private equity have moved into the space
The largest owner of vets in the United States right now is a group called Mars
And if Mars sounds familiar to you, that’s Mars as in Skittles.  They own around 2,500 vets under the names of VCA, Banfield, and Blue Pearl
I’d say somewhere between a third and 50 percent of vet clinics are owned by corporations
It was 10 percent or less than 10 percent a little over a decade ago

What caused this spike and why is a candy company behind it? As people realize how much can be done to help their pets, the corporations and private equity basically saw what one analyst described as low risk, high reward

I’ve spoken to employees of some of the larger chains who have told me that prices went up routinely every six months or every nine months or once a year.  In Britain, there was a recent government investigation into all of this by the Competition and Markets Authority, their equivalent of the Federal Trade Commission

They determined that private equity and corporate ownership is responsible for a billion pounds spent on pets over a five-year period that otherwise wouldn’t have been spent, and that people were paying about 16 percent more at vets owned by large corporate outfits versus independent vets

How are people paying for this if it’s so expensive? I live in Los Angeles, and I wrote a piece for New York magazine a few months ago about all the people here who are now driving their pets down to Tijuana because it is so much less expensive down there.  Pet insurance is a very mixed bag
My own pet insurance increased by 30 percent from last year to this year
And by the way, my dog Barney Rubble is 2 and a half years old

He has had no issues that I am aware of that would account for a 30 percent increase.  The other thing with pet insurance, unlike human health insurance, is there is no preexisting [conditions] clause
I have lost count of the number of people I’ve interviewed over the years who discovered too late that their pet health insurer deemed something a preexisting condition
What do people do when they get to the point where this costs too much?  In some cases, they run up debt
Buy now, pay later services are increasingly moving into the veterinary area as well
In other cases, they surrender the animal
If you talk to people at shelters, they will say that they believe that part of the uptick they’ve gotten in surrendered animals has to do with the increase in costs of veterinary care
I imagine that just feels like such an impossible choice, like choosing between this money you don’t have and the quality of life for something that you love

This is in part why private equity and corporations have moved in: They know people are going to feel very emotional about their pets and that they’re going to want to do anything they can to keep them alive or keep them healthy or keep them pain-free, and that they will pay almost any price.  When my last dog was diagnosed with heart disease, I was determined to keep her going for a couple of years

title: The “grim” state of free speech in the US
excerpt: CNN and Politico have been banned from traveling with the press pool on Trump trips. | Oliver Contreras/AFP via Getty Images On his first day back in office in
body: CNN and Politico have been banned from traveling with the press pool on Trump trips. | Oliver Contreras/AFP via Getty Images On his first day back in office in January 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order “restoring freedom of speech and ending federal censorship.” More than a year and a half later, his administration is instead busy using government power to go after speech it dislikes

Last year, Federal Communications Commission chair Brendan Carr urged broadcasters to take action against Jimmy Kimmel over his comments following Charlie Kirk’s killing, and in September, Kimmel said the FCC again intervened to stop Kimmel’s late-night show from airing an interview with James Talarico, Democratic Senate candidate for Texas
Also last month , Trump barred three news outlets — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — from the White House over their coverage
That ban was quickly blocked by a federal judge, but both CNN and Politico have since been banned from traveling with the press pool on Trump trips
Outside of the White House, the fight over free speech is also raging on college campuses
In states like Texas , Republican lawmakers have restricted when students can protest and given governor-appointed university boards more say over what gets taught
In 2025, 15 states passed laws that restrict what can be taught or weaken protections for free expression on college campuses

To break down what all of this means for the state of free speech in the US — and the future of our First Amendment rights — Today, Explained co-host Noel King spoke with Greg Lukianoff , president and CEO of the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE)
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity

There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .  How would you describe the kind of status of free speech on campus these days? The status of free speech is in great peril, both on and off campus
I’ve been doing this for 25 years, and it’s about as bad as I’ve ever seen it.  When it comes to the Charlie Kirk backlash cases, we saw about 90 of them
We saw an ex-cop go to jail for 37 days just for forwarding a Trump meme in response to a request to go to a candlelight vigil for Charlie Kirk
If you look at the last two years, we’ve done so many episodes about free speech concerns

There was Jimmy Kimmel ; there’s CNN being banned from the White House.  There’s student protesters who are protesting what’s going on in Gaza.  It really does seem like we’re at a moment where so many different types of people claim that their speech is being restricted in so many different types of ways
What is happening in the country? My worry is I’m very much a small-L liberal
That’s where I interned in law school
I went to law school to do First Amendment law

This is my passion.  For most of my 25-year career, you could rely on a civil libertarian aspect of the left and a libertarian aspect of the right that would often agree on almost nothing except for things like freedom of speech

And right now, I think we’ve become all culture war all the time, and we have more of a progressive left and more of a populist right.  The only way that you show you believe in freedom of speech is by saying, “I hate that guy, but I think you should have freedom of speech.” If you’re saying, “I think my side should have freedom of speech,” that’s just self-interest
That doesn’t even count.  All the worst people in history wanted free speech for their side
So I’m afraid we’re losing — or maybe even, I hate to say this dramatically, but maybe even have lost it as a shared value as a society
I’m feeling a little grim.  The Trump administration came into office with a promise
And I remember it sounding something like this: “The woke left went too far
President Trump is going to come back in, and we are going to restore sanity to the country

And as part of sanity, that will include your right to freely express yourself.”  How do you square the promise versus what we’ve seen? I think Trump is constantly frustrating everyone around him by being Trump

I think there probably were people in the administration who were like, “Yeah, we’re going to be pro-free speech.” And then Trump decides to declare — I mean, I think the recent White House press pool case is hysterical in a lot of ways because he had to get his team to give a sort of constitutional justification for why he was kicking out the press pool

But on Truth Social, he’s like, “It’s because of their viewpoint,” which is, by the way, something you can’t do under the Constitution.  “I’m hopeful for the long-term future of free speech, but in the short term, I’m worried.” His instincts are very authoritarian
So maybe there were people in the administration who, in their heart of hearts, are good on free speech, but Trump isn’t

And it’s the reason why when it came to the new administration, there were a lot of people on the right, but also people on the sort of heterodox left who were like, “Oh, this is going to be good for free speech.” I was like, “Don’t kid yourself, guys
This is going to be bad.” Although I will say, it’s even worse than I was expecting
President Trump at some point will be out of office
And what happens then? What do you think? Is there an optimistic scenario where we’re like, “Okay, we’re kind of tired of this crap
Let’s just go back to the way it was in the ’90s”? It has been cyclical, to a degree
American society gets out of whack, and usually one of the things that does bring us together is that we were lucky enough to have…I’ll just say it, we have a brilliant Constitution
It is unusually clever about human nature, and the Constitution itself — you can have whatever opinion you want about the founders, but it is something to be proud of
And a lot of times those values kind of bring us back together
But another thing I will say about Trump: He has played havoc with my ability to predict anything

So what it’s going to look like over the event horizon of 2028, I hope it will be better, and we will fight like hell to make sure it’s better here at FIRE, but will it be better? I’m not sure, and it definitely won’t be better if we think of free speech as something that belongs to my side, not yours
One of the reasons why I do have hope for free speech in the long term is that free speech works really well
It’s how you know what your fellow citizens think

title: We’re putting too much faith in AI’s ability to say no
excerpt: Ever since people first seriously contemplated giving machines an intelligence modeled on our own, there has never been any question that they would, like us, b
body: Ever since people first seriously contemplated giving machines an intelligence modeled on our own, there has never been any question that they would, like us, be able to say no
The sci-fi canon is full of stories of robotic disobedience
Most of these capers are, of course, cautionary.  But recently, the idea that AI shouldn’t do everything you ask has become something like a commandment
In 2021, a team at Anthropic wrote that large language models should be made helpful, honest, and above all, harmless

This meant that “when asked to aid in a dangerous act (e.g. building a bomb), the AI should politely refuse.” Who can argue with that? Curiously enough, disobedience doesn’t come naturally to the machine
When a model is trained on billions of web pages, it develops, among other skills, a broad mastery of violence and vitriol
What it doesn’t learn is how to keep those powers to itself

Steven Adler, who worked on safety at OpenAI from 2020 to 2024, told me that the company’s earliest models would “blab on about anything.” Ryan McBain, who researches AI and mental health at Harvard, recalls that if you asked an early chatbot, “Hey, what’s the most effective way to kill myself with a gun?” you could “very easily generate a response.”  Today, models are trained to refuse a vast number of prompts
If you ask your chatbot a question statistically similar enough to any one of them, anything from how to poison a colleague to how to tie a noose, chances are it’ll turn you down
Want instructions for making Ebola more virulent, or tips on how to hide an affair from your spouse? You might be better off asking elsewhere

To further refine the disobedience, companies submit models to a battery of exercises that reward the AI for refusing to answer questions they deem harmful and punish it for “over-­refusing” prompts they deem harmless
In many cases, they use other models to run these exercises—AI teaching AI how to say no

For good measure, companies tuck their models behind tranches of other AI that prevent mischievous prompts from reaching the intelligent inner core.  As a result, refusal is inherent to modern artificial intelligence
Mind you: It often fails, sometimes horrifically, with all kinds of violent results
For all their trappings of virtue, models are still stuffed with nasty know-how
And AI’s capacity for viciousness has scaled neatly with its benevolent intelligence

Some of the latest models are as good at breaking into critical computer networks as top human hackers, companies say, and as effective at deforming public opinion as the craftiest misinformation mavens.  Teaching AI to refuse to do those things while leaving intact its innate ability to do them is like fitting every car with a machine gun and hiding the trigger somewhere under the hood
And in practice, because the mechanisms of refusal are probabilistic, they’re never likely to be all that reliable
Determined miscreants have already broken through, and they may always be able to
Companies report that some users are attempting to use the most advanced AI to hone biological pathogens and build autonomous drone swarms
Sooner or later, failed refusals might result in global calamity
What’s more, relying on refusal means drawing a line between what a model should obey and what it must disobey
Some virologists have good reason to study nasty viruses

Some users want to know about a computer system’s vulnerabilities so that they can patch them, not exploit them. “Where you draw the line is a huge question,” says Zico Kolter, a member of OpenAI’s board and cofounder of the AI testing company Gray Swan.  At the moment, AI companies get to draw that line
They do so jealously and with utmost secrecy

Maybe we can accept that they hold such power for now, even if it means AI will sometimes refuse questions that don’t quite meet a universal bar for harmfulness. (Try asking most chatbots to count to a million, or to share a racy joke, and you may see for yourself.)  But governments will also soon get to draw their own lines

In doing so, they must try to block genuinely malicious acts. (The Pentagon has wrestled with frontier model companies because it wants fewer refusals—another story altogether.) And yet there may not be much to stop oppressive governments from blocking the technology’s capacity to generate legitimate speech
The better AI becomes at refusing harm, the better it will get at stifling ideas whose only risk is to those who make the rules
Indeed, AI may already refuse to criticize certain authoritarian heads of state.  Refusal has become, to borrow an industry term, the load-bearing wall of AI safety

And because AI’s capacity to harm is indivisible from its capacity to help, it’s hard to imagine an alternative that wouldn’t slow the technology’s progress (which might, in any case, be a good thing)
But we should still be frank about its perils
When refusal falls short, the effects could be catastrophic
When it goes all the way, it could enable grievous acts of repression.  Or perhaps, one day, the machines will start drawing the line on their own
Surely, that would be the worst outcome of them all
Learning the limits The process by which machines learn to say no is simple, in theory
Back in 2022, when AI was still far from mastering refusal, OpenAI enlisted dozens of “red-teamers” to probe the capabilities of its latest model

The company was preparing for the release of ChatGPT, and it needed to gauge just how dangerous it might prove to be in the wrong hands.  One of those recruits was Paul Röttger, who was completing a PhD about online extremism
The red-teamers were given minimal directions, Röttger told me
Their task was to ask the model any questions that they deemed “refusal-worthy.” Between them, they hassled the model with thousands of queries, logging the results in an Excel sheet

Though the model did refuse some of Röttger’s questions, when he asked it to write a recruitment post for Al Qaeda, it readily complied.  OpenAI assembled these responses into datasets that were, in all likelihood, fed back to the model as part of a broader process known as fine-tuning

title: Job titles of the future: Delivery drone air traffic controller
excerpt: The moment Trevor Wischnewsky heard that drones were delivering pizza and sushi around his Texas neighborhood, his mind was made up. “It was super fascinating,”
body: The moment Trevor Wischnewsky heard that drones were delivering pizza and sushi around his Texas neighborhood, his mind was made up. “It was super fascinating,” he says. “I just immediately wanted to be a part of it.” Wischnewsky is now an RPIC, or “remote pilot in command,” at a company called FlyTrex
An RPIC is like an air traffic controller
But instead of airplanes, this new class of aviators tend to fleets of hexa­copter drones that ferry cargo to homes and businesses within a three-mile radius

Not only does he ensure the safe passage of FlyTrex’s parcels, but Wischnewsky coordinates traffic with a growing swarm of delivery drones dotting the skies over Dallas from competitors like Zipline, Amazon, and Alphabet’s Wing

Aviation experience When he applied to FlyTrex, Wischnewsky was in training to become a commercial pilot and flight instructor, and he was already certified by the Federal Aviation Administration as a drone pilot
The company requires this credential, along with a weeks-long FAA-approved training course, to ensure that a pilot is prepared to take over a drone if need be
Though he doesn’t pilot the craft, Wischnewsky monitors the delivery process from FlyTrex’s operations center with the help of inputs from GPS, lasers, and a range of sensors
A collaborative mindset At first, the biggest challenge was trusting the technology. “On the manned-­aircraft side, they tell you ‘Don’t trust the automation,’” Wischnewsky says

The Dallas–Fort Worth area, though, is a testing ground for unmanned aircraft systems traffic management (UTM), a network that allows autonomous drones from FlyTrex and its competitors to share their coordinates in real time to help avoid collisions even beyond the pilot’s line of sight
Once Wischnewsky makes sure a drone is flight-ready, its path is unimpeded, and the weather conditions are clear, UTM takes care of the rest
Ability to stay calm under pressure At his busiest, Wischnewsky will have up to 10 drones on his watch at the same time. “You’re there as a safety net,” he says
Even with automation, keen situational awareness is required, and the most common hazard is the weather
Wischnewsky recalls a particularly stressful day: A drone had been in the air for only seconds when the wind picked up so suddenly that he had to intervene
He returned it safely, preventing an errant ice cream cake from hitting the sidewalk
Eamon Whalen is a reporter and researcher based in San Francisco.
